title: Introduction to Flight
scope: Following are the scope and objective of this course: a. Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion. b. Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures, propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions. c. Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems. d. Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering.
description: This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems, and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering.

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
scope: The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of practical biology.
description: Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant tissues and Cell cycle analysis.
makeup_policy: If a student misses the Mid-Semester or Comprehensive Examination due to a genuine reason (serious medical causes leading to hospitalization (certified by doctor from BITS medical center), personal/family emergencies) there exists a provision to apply for make-up. Prior permission must be taken from the Instructor-in-Charge, before applying for make-up. Make-up decisions will be made on a case-by-case basis and only genuine cases as determined by the Departmental team will be considered. No Make-Up will be granted for quiz and assignments.

description.supporting_text: This course is intended to offer an introduction to the world of Biological Chemistry. The course deals with the structure, properties, and significance of the major groups of biochemical compounds (amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and lipids), the bioenergetics, enzyme mechanisms and regulation of the central metabolic pathways. Efforts will be made to include the recent advances and methodologies related to biochemistry. This would help students going for higher level activities, appreciation of biochemical problems, evaluation and problem solving.

title: Microbiology
scope: This course deals with the structure, physiology, genetics and growth of various microorganisms as well as their control. Emphasis will be given on microbes and their role in human health, environment and industry.
description: Introduction and classification of microbes; isolation, cultivation, physiological and biochemical characterization of microbes; structure, physiology and genetics of microbial cell; synthetic microbiology; host parasite relationship; physical chemical methods of controlling microbes; antimicrobial drugs; clinical microbiology; microbiology of soil, water and food; and related lab components.

title: CELL BIOLOGY
scope: A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure, intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms and related experimental procedures. The topics learned in this course will also be foundational for advanced courses in cell and molecular biology, as well as genetics and developmental biology.

title: INTEGRATED BIOLOGY
scope: Being the second course on General Biology, the course exposes the students to the foundational aspects as described above. At the end of the course, the student will have developed a basic understanding of the evolutionary processes, rationale for taxonomic arrangements and familiarity of selected, representative members of the major kingdoms of living organisms. Further, the student will also become aware of how knowledge of biology (both botany and zoology) is applied for benefit of mankind and other organisms.
description: The course intends to bridge the gap and open new vistas to students taking up biology. The course covers two tracks, essentially. The first track introduces the student to the ordering that helps biologists to actually study the vast diversity of the living ing world. This track would encompass questions related to the origin and evolutionary pathways followed in nature, as well as the methods followed by biologists to systematically categorize and document them. The second track highlights the uses and applications applications of biology in everyday life – whether in the economic or in the social realms. Together, the course projects the subject in a way from which the student can choose and implement his biological knowledge vis vis-à-vis his/her interests.

title: RECOMBINANT DNA TECHNOLOGY
scope: Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology.
description: The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation. Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems and whole genome approaches will be covered.

scope.supporting_text: Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology.

description.supporting_text: The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation. Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems and whole genome approaches will be covered.

title: Plant Physiology
scope: This course attempts to make the students aware of the major features of physiological aspects of plant system. Emphasis will be given to understand the plant tissue systems, water and mineral nutrient uptake and their distribution, mechanism of transpiration and photosynthate transport, the role of hormones in plant growth & developmental and mechanism of flowering.
description: Basic functional processes in plants; Plant tissue system, Plant-water relations, Gaseous exchange, Stomatal regulations, Mineral nutrition and absorption, Transport of material, Growth and development, Hormones and Plant Growth Regulators, Photoperiodism, Vernalization, Stress Physiology and related lab components.
makeup_policy: Make-up decisions will be made on a case-by-case basis and only genuine cases as determined by the Departmental team will be considered. No make-up for Quizzes and Practical Assignments.

title: Biomolecular Modeling
scope: The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and structural biology. It describes the functionality, advantages, and limitations of standard computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data in a research or industry laboratory environment.
description: Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding, Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice models, usage of modeling packages.
makeup_policy: Make up will be given on genuine grounds as determined by the Instructor-in-charge

title: ENZYMOLOGY
scope: This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology and will create research interest among the students.
description: Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.

title: Molecular Immunology
scope: The course intends to familiarize the students with modern concepts in immunology. The endeavor will be to highlight concepts in immunology, which would have an influence on understanding the fascinating entity which comprises the body’s immune system and ancillary procedure of therapy.
description: The course will deal extensively with topics like molecular basis of T and B cell antigen recognition and activation. Immunity to microbes and diseases caused by humoral and cell mediated immune responses will be covered and emphasis placed on congenital and acquired immuno-deficiencies. Advanced topics like antibody engineering will be discussed with the help of review articles.
makeup_policy: No make-ups without prior intimation or only in case of hospitalization.

title: Microbiology
scope: This course deals with the structure, physiology, genetics and growth of various microorganisms as well as their control. Emphasis will be given on microbes and their role in human health, environment and industry.
description: Introduction and classification of microbes; isolation, cultivation, physiological and biochemical characterization of microbes; structure, physiology and genetics of microbial cell; synthetic microbiology; host parasite relationship; physical chemical methods of controlling microbes; antimicrobial drugs; clinical microbiology; microbiology of soil, water and food; and related lab components.
makeup_policy: If a student misses the Mid-Semester or Comprehensive Examination due to a genuine reason (serious medical causes leading to hospitalization (certified by doctor from BITS medical center), personal/family emergencies) there exists a provision to apply for make-up. Prior permission must be taken from the Instructor-in-Charge, before applying for make-up. Make-up decisions will be made on a case-by- case basis and only genuine cases as determined by the Departmental team will be considered. No Make-Up will be granted for quiz, assignments and Lab components.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL BIOTECHNOLOGY AND WASTE
scope: The major objective of this course is to impart knowledge on application of biotechnological processes for betterment of environment. This course is designed to make the student understand the various biological phenomena, which can be exploited to save environment from eventual deterioration.
description: Application of biotechnology to the management of environmental problems. Biotechnology for enhanced plant and animal production through biological insecticides, herbicides resistance, mineral cycling, conservation of genetic resources and biological nitrogen fixation. Use of biotechnological processes for pollution control, bioremediation of toxicants and treatment of domestic and industrial wastes. Ethical issues related with the release of genetically modified organism.
makeup_policy: No make-up except in case of hospitalization.

title: BIOSTATISTICS & BIOMODELING
scope: The student would learn how to collect data suitable for statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of significance.
description: Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.
makeup_policy: Make-up will be given only in case of hospitalization cases and under emergency conditions for which all documents need to be provided. It is expected that students shall avoid misuse of this feature. The decision of IC/ Course Instructor will be final.

Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.

title: INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL SCIENCES
scope: The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of practical biology.
description: Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant tissues and Cell cycle analysis.
makeup_policy: If a student misses the Mid-Semester or Comprehensive Examination due to a genuine reason (serious medical causes leading to hospitalization (certified by doctor from BITS medical center), personal/family emergencies) there exists a provision to apply for make-up. Prior permission must be taken from the Instructor-in-Charge, before applying for make-up. Make-up decisions will be made on a case-by-case basis and only genuine cases as determined by the Departmental team will be considered. No Make-Up will be granted for quiz and assignments.

title: ENZYMOLOGY
scope: This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology and will create research interest among the students.
description: Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.

title: Food Biotechnology
scope: The aim of this course is providing the students with basic knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors. These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.
description: The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed.
makeup_policy: No make-up will be granted without a genuine case. A certificate from authenticated doctor must accompany the makeup application (only prescriptions/ vouchers for medicines will not be sufficient). Prior permission from IC is strongly recommended. No makeup for in class assignments and quizzes.

source.supporting_text: The aim of this course is providing the students with basic knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors. These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed.

title: Ph.D. SEMINAR
scope: The aim of this course is to develop student’s expertise in the art of oral presentation of his/her research work. It also aims to train students in the art of presentation of their scientific work at seminars etc. 2. Operation of the course: The student should immediately interact with his/her supervisor(s)/mentor and decide the topics for the seminar to be presented during the semester. Each semester, the DRC will organize seminars by Ph.D. students to which members of the DAC (as also members of relevant departments) will be invited. A student will give at least two seminars. In case supervisor(s)/mentor desires, he/she may ask his/her students to present more than two seminars also, and he/she would then proportionally assign marks for each seminar and record the Grades/marks in evaluation form broadly in two components. Each component may have more than one seminar.

title: STUDY IN ADVANCE TOPIC II
scope: The course aims at covering topics in advanced areas of professional interest and will be conducted on self-study and seminar basis. The course is specially designed to provide an opportunity to the students for development of their academic skills and logical thinking through open ended advanced study oriented activities. As a part of education, this course follows a method of learning and, therefore, the student's actual day-to-day task involvement would constitute the central thread of the learning process. The evaluation will recognize this aspect by demanding day-to-day productivity, punctuality and final achievement of the student. 3. Operation of the course: The plan of work for each student will be decided by the respective Instructors/supervisors. Each student should adhere to the plan of work decided for and should regularly monitor the progress of the course accordingly. The final report encompassing critical review of the material studied will be submitted to the Instructor-in-charge through Departmental Committee on Academics (DCA) by the end of the class work.
description: In this course students will be assigned study work in advanced areas of professional interest. Each student will work under the overall supervision and guidance of a faculty member and will in the end submit a project report encompassing critical review of the material studied. The organization and evaluation of the course would be achieved through seminars, group discussions, project report etc. The course will be conducted by the team of teachers who provide guidance for study work.

title: ENGINEERING GRAPHICS
scope: Computerized drafting provides accurate and easily modifiable graphics entities, easy data storage and retrieval facility and enhances creativity. Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:  Read and interpret engineering drawings  Identify the three principal projection planes  Draw 2-dimensional orthographic projections from given 3-dimensional views  Create an isometric drawing using AutoCAD  Comprehend orthographic and multiview projection  Apply the concept of cutting planes to create the various types of sectional views  Become conversant with appropriate use of AutoCAD software for drafting.
description: The course includes fundamentals and techniques of technical drawing and standard practices of the same so that design ideas can be adequately communicated and produced. It introduces students to the theories of projection and the concepts of engineering drawing using the most widely used CAD application software, AutoCAD. Basic AutoCAD 2023 commands will also be introduced. The course covers the following topics: Introduction to AutoCAD basic commands; theory of projections; orthographic projections; isometric projections; projection of points, lines, planes and solids; section of solids; developments of surfaces.

title: Thermodynamics
scope: Thermodynamics deals with energy, matter, and the laws governing their interactions. • To learn usefulness of laws of thermodynamics in the design of processes, devices, and systems involving effective utilization of energy and matter. • To understand the fundamentals and concepts of the laws of thermodynamics as applied to control mass and control volume systems. • To apply the fundamentals and concepts of the laws of thermodynamics to control mass and control volume systems and analyze them. • To examine the performance of engineering devices in light of the laws of thermodynamics. 3. To define, understand, apply and analyze the concept of irreversibility and availability to thermodynamic systems and to evaluate second law efficiency of thermodynamics systems and devices.
description: Concepts and laws of thermodynamics; thermodynamic properties; applications to closed and open systems; entropy and entropy generation; availability.

title: Science, Technology and Modernity
scope: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.

scope: The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. title: PROCESS ENGINEERING
scope: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical aspects of pharmaceutical engineering, with a focus on key unit operations involved in the development and manufacturing of pharmaceutical formulations. It covers a wide range of processes including size reduction and separation, drying, evaporation, distillation, mixing, filtration, centrifugation, extraction, compression, crystallization, and materials of plant construction. The course emphasizes the selection, operation, and application of various equipment used in the pharmaceutical industry.
description: Basic concepts related to heat transfer, mass transfer and flow of fluid, processes and equipment involved in extraction and filtration; mixing and granulation; size reduction and classification, evaporation and distillation, drying and crystallization, humidification and dehumidification. Materials of construction. Theory of compression and consolidation of solids.

title: Environmental Studies
scope: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas.
description: Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact assessment.

scope.supporting_text: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas.

description.supporting_text: Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact assessment.

title: Foundations of Data Structures and Algorithms
scope: A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera- tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks, queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute- force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in- cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis. Objectives • Apply basic data structures (stacks, queues, linked lists, trees) to solve programming prob- lems. • Implement advanced data structures (graphs, balanced search trees, hash tables, priority queues) for complex applications. • Use algorithmic techniques (brute-force, greedy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming) to address real-world challenges. • Develop skills to design and implement data abstractions for problem-solving.

title: Introduction to Engineering Design
scope: The scope and objectives of the course are as follows: 1. Apply key elements of the design process and scientific principles to create detailed design of a product that meets engineering requirements and standards. 2. Generate and interpret engineering technical drawings of parts and assemblies according to engineering design standards; and 3. Use CAD software to generate a computer model of a well-defined part or assembly.
description: This course provides students with a foundation in engineering design practice and prepares them for discipline-specific advanced courses in engineering design. Students will gain experience in the use of digital design techniques and management of larger open-ended, team-based engineering design tasks in a project-based learning environment. Students will learn to create detailed designs of real-world products and systems by applying design thinking and scientific principles. Students will learn a range of design techniques to contextualize, evaluate, and communicate designs, from generating ideas via sketching to development of digital models and detailed technical drawings that meet the international standards. Students will develop foundation skills in computer-aided design (CAD) techniques to generate 3D models of products and assemblies and learn to integrate them in augmented and virtual reality tools. 2. Course Contents: Engineering Design process, Introduction to Engineering Drawing, Introduction to Orthographic Projections, Projections of points, lines, planes, and solid objects, Sectional views, Manufacturing processes and materials, Fits and Tolerances, Isometric Drawing, Introduction to Solid Modelling, Assembly drawings

title: GAME THEORY & ITS APPLICATIONS
scope: Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.
description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Robotics
scope: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation. _
description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.

source.supporting_text: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation. _

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.

title: FUZZY LOGIC & APPLICATIONS
scope: The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts of fuzzy sets, fuzzy relations, fuzzy logic, and fuzzy reasoning, along with their applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems, artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. Emphasis is placed on developing analytical, computational, and problem-solving skills through real-world applications. Each student is required to undertake a project involving the application of fuzzy logic, which may be study-oriented, computer-oriented, simulation-based, or model-based, and provides an opportunity to explore research articles and recent developments in fuzzy logic and its applications.
description: Fuzzy sets, fuzzy binary relations, fuzzy logic, fuzzy reasoning, applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems, artificial intelligence etc.

title: Human Computer Interaction
scope: At the completion of this course, students will be able to: • Understand the concepts and theories of human-AI interaction. Furthermore, they will be able to explain basic concepts from the relevant theories in cognitive and social sciences. (LO1) • Illustrate and compare methods of “user-centered engineering (UCE)”, involving future users in various stages of the design and development process of AI systems. (LO2) • Apply “user-centered” methods appropriately, as a team; as part of design, development, and evaluation of AI systems. (LO3) • Apply ethics procedures for user studies (e.g., privacy, consent) and FATE principles in design of prototype based AI systems. (LO4) • Describe the perspectives and values of multiple stakeholders at different stages of the user-centered engineering process (requirements, design, and evaluation). (LO5)
description: Introduction to HCI in the AI era; Understanding People: Perception, Motor control, Cognition, Needs, and Experience; User Research: Interviews, Field research, and Survey research; Understanding Interaction: Usability Engineering, Information and control, Dialogue, Tool use, Automation, and Rationality; User Interfaces: Input devices, Displays, Interaction techniques, and Reality-based interaction; Design: Cognition, Practice, and Processes; Engineering: Systems, Design engineering, Safety and risk, and Computational representations and models; Evaluation: Analytical methods, Think-aloud studies, and Experiment.

title: Introduction to Gender Studies
scope: To develop the knowledge necessary for addressing issues of gender equity and understanding gender roles. The course would help students get a greater insight into women’s rights, their role in shaping political, social, economic and cultural institutions. Emphasis would be laid on understanding the dynamics of gender relations in educational institutions, work and home. The course would further aim at gender sensitization in the context of societal stratifications.
description: Introduction to Gender Studies and Feminist Movements; Theories of Gender; Sex, Gender and Sexuality; Social Construction of Gender; Intersectionality and Social Location; Marriage, Family and Gender Discrimination; Gender and Labour Politics; Productivity and Labour Issues; Unpaid Domestic Work and Gendered Labour; Globalization, Global Assembly Line, Care Work and Emotion Labour; Ideal Worker Norm and Second Shift; Gender Discrimination in the Workplace; Media Representations and Male Gaze; Theories of Masculinity; Gender Based Violence.

title: Introduction to Nano Science
scope: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.
description: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.

title: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment
scope: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3 modules as decribed below. o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).
description: This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment, and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology.

title: [Flexible Manufacturing Systems]
scope: In recent years the manufacturing industries are facing problems of survival. They find it difficult to maintain a long term competitive advantage due to uncertainty in environmental conditions. The ideal production system for such environment is Flexible Manufacturing Systems (FMS), which are considered to meet the demand for a variety of products with improvement of productivity in mid-volume manufacturing. This course will highlight the fundamentals of FMS and modelling for design, planning and control of FMS.
description: Introduction of CAD/CAM systems, overview of FMS, system hardware and general functions, material handling system, work holding systems, cutting tools and tool management, physical planning of system, software structure functions and description, cleaning and automated inspection, communications and computer networks for manufacturing, quantification of flexibility, human factors in manufacturing, FMS and CIM in action (case studies), justification of FMS, modelling for design, planning and operation of FMS.

scope.supporting_text: In recent years the manufacturing industries are facing problems of survival. They find it difficult to maintain a long term competitive advantage due to uncertainty in environmental conditions. The ideal production system for such environment is Flexible Manufacturing Systems (FMS), which are considered to meet the demand for a variety of products with improvement of productivity in mid-volume manufacturing. This course will highlight the fundamentals of FMS and modelling for design, planning and control of FMS.

description.supporting_text: Introduction of CAD/CAM systems, overview of FMS, system hardware and general functions, material handling system, work holding systems, cutting tools and tool management, physical planning of system, software structure functions and description, cleaning and automated inspection, communications and computer networks for manufacturing, quantification of flexibility, human factors in manufacturing, FMS and CIM in action (case studies), justification of FMS, modelling for design, planning and operation of FMS.

title: Pattern Recognition
scope: Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to verification of signatures, and from analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of fingerprints and human blood cells. Currently, pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces- sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them.
description: This is a first course on Pattern recognition. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition. It goes on to discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation and description and finally the object recognition. During the course, a flavour of matlab programming will also be given.

course_codes.supporting_text: Course No. : BITS F464 / CS U311

title: BIOETHICS AND BIOSAFETY
scope: This course is designed to create an awareness on the basic concepts of biosafety and bioethics that are essential for various branches of science which has had an great impact on quality of life and regulations governing the experimentations on transgenic organisms and plants, prenatal diagnosis and related social issues, handling and disposal of hazardous materials, environmental pollution concerns and ethics in need based experimentation on animals and plants, would be addressed. Emphasis will also be made on health care related issues.

title: New Venture Creation
instructor: (Pilani & All Campuses)             : Prof. Jyoti Tikoria + Dr. Paul Lopez
scope: NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?
description: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.

title: Introduction to Large Language Models
scope: By the end of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and apply prompt engineering techniques to control the behavior of LLMs. b. Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for combining LLMs with external knowledge bases. c. Fine-tune LLMs for specific tasks using publicly available models. d. Leverage tool calling to enable LLMs to interact with external systems and APIs. e. Design and implement multi-agent workflows where multiple LLMs interact to solve complex tasks. f. Implement guardrails to ensure the safe and ethical deployment of LLMs in production environments. g. Understand the internal architecture of LLMs and the entire life cycle of LLM Training and Fine-Tuning. h. Evaluate the performance and accuracy of LLM-powered applications using appropriate metrics. i. Understand the principles of inference for deploying LLM models efficiently at scale.
description: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs); prompt engineering techniques (e.g., zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), autonomous prompt optimization; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector databases, multi-modal RAG methods; tool and function calling; multi-agent workflows (memory, planning, action, reflection); safety, guardrails, reliability; LLM-based evaluation, human evaluation; life cycle of LLM training, LLM architecture, fine-tuning LLMs using supervised learning or reinforcement learning; inference optimization; Mechanistic Interpretability; real-world case-studies
makeup_policy: Make-up will be granted only in genuine cases based on individual’s need and circumstances.

scope.supporting_text: By the end of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and apply prompt engineering techniques to control the behavior of LLMs. b. Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for combining LLMs with external knowledge bases. c. Fine-tune LLMs for specific tasks using publicly available models. d. Leverage tool calling to enable LLMs to interact with external systems and APIs. e. Design and implement multi-agent workflows where multiple LLMs interact to solve complex tasks. f. Implement guardrails to ensure the safe and ethical deployment of LLMs in production environments. g. Understand the internal architecture of LLMs and the entire life cycle of LLM Training and Fine-Tuning. h. Evaluate the performance and accuracy of LLM-powered applications using appropriate metrics. i. Understand the principles of inference for deploying LLM models efficiently at scale.

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
scope: The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
description: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, background of previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating the intermediate milestones and the estimated time to achieve the same along with
description: This course deals with the research and development work in assigned areas of professional interest. Each student will work under the overall guidance and supervision of a faculty member/professional. The course must end with a well defined Final Report outlining all the investigations, achievements and conclusions at the end of each semester. source.supporting_text: Evaluation in this course is essentially individual oriented. The various instruments of evaluation along with the weightage of components are given below: Component Weightage Week in which due Viva-I 15 5th week Mid. sem. Written report 15 10th week Mid sem. presentation 15 10th week Viva-II 15 15th week Final Dissertation* 25 Last day of class work Final viva-voce* 15 Actual date announced by DRC *Final viva-voce examination and evaluation of the Dissertation is to be jointly done by the Supervisor and the examiner appointed by the DRC. The other components are to be evaluated by the supervisor and the details are to be made available to the examiner at the time of final viva. Supervisor will send the copy of Dissertation report to the examiner well in advance. Before sending he should check the contents as per checklist and sign the ‘Certificate’ page. The evaluation will recognize the day-to-day work involvement and punctuality of the student in his work. Evaluation in various components shall take into account work progress and achievements, technical/professional competence, documentation and expression, initiative and originality, punctuality and reliability, self-reliance, and acquisition of special skills. The student should extend full cooperation to his supervisor and interact with him in advance about the time, venue and mode of each evaluation. He should be in constant touch with his supervisor. Supervisor may require his student to sign the attendance sheet before a particular time on each working day. Grading will be done mainly on the basis of the progress made towards attaining the overall objectives of the Dissertation. The supervisor shall evaluate various prescribed components of evaluation before the submission of final Dissertation. He/she should seek utmost participation of examiner by inviting him to the various seminars. Supervisor should maintain all pertinent records of his student. The final report and performance in the final viva are to be jointly evaluated by the Supervisor and examiner appointed by the DRC. title: Research Methodology I
scope: The objective of this course is to train the Ph.D. students in the art of research and involves various related aspects. This course helps the students in gaining deeper understanding of fundamental concepts and acquiring the techniques of communicating at a professional level. 3. Operation of the course: All Ph.D. students will be assigned an on-going project generally drawn from the core courses of the first/higher degree under the guidance of a senior faculty member. Several practice lectures will be held in which each student will be given an opportunity. Besides the technical contents, the basic important pointsto be focused during the lectures are. a) Planning b) Oral communication c) Audience awareness d) Style of presentation. Each Ph.D. student will submit a Mid-Semester Report and a final report, which will include the following. a) Outline of lectures delivered or other related activities. b) References and bibliography of literature consulted c) Conclusions.

scope: Students will learn to put their design ideas in the form of drawings and further go on to create a prototype in the workshop. Engineering drawings and hands-on fabrication are blended into a foundational design course. It transitions students from design ideas to theoretical drawing techniques and finally to real-world prototyping, thereby imparting both software & shop-floor competencies.

Engineering drawings and hands-on fabrication are blended into a foundational design course. It transitions students from design ideas to theoretical drawing techniques and finally to real-world prototyping, thereby imparting both software & shop-floor competencies.

title: Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation
scope: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to: (i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali- bration, and uncertainty. (ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif- ferent domains. (iii) Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. (iv) Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and validation. (v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering principles. (vi) Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen- tation and technical reporting.
description: This course introduces scientific and engineering inquiry through the principles of measurement and experimentation. It covers fundamental concepts, such as accuracy, precision, calibration, error analysis, and uncertainty, as well as the hands-on use of sophisticated instruments across multiple disciplines. The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. It emphasizes experimental design, hypothesis formulation, and experimental validation. It also focuses on correlating measurements with real-world problems, documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration to ethical practices in experimentation.

title: Introduction to MEMS
scope: The course introduces the basic concepts in MEMS (Micro Electromechanical Systems) with a view to address a class of students from science and engineering disciplines. The discussion on topics like MEMS design, Microfabrication, Microfluidics, Sensors and actuators have been structured in the course plan. The objective of the course is to equip the students from various aspects and with basic knowledge of the area of MEMS.
description: Micro electro mechanical systems (MEMS), devices and technologies. Micro-machining and mi- crofabrication techniques. Transduction mechanisms and modeling in different energy domains. Analysis of micromachined capacitive, piezoresistive and thermal sensors/actuators and applica- tions. Computer- aided design for MEMS layout, fabrication and analysis.

scope.supporting_text: This course is designed to create an awareness on the basic concepts of biosafety and bioethics that are essential for various branches of science which has had an great impact on quality of life and regulations governing the experimentations on transgenic organisms and plants, prenatal diagnosis and related social issues, handling and disposal of hazardous materials, environmental pollution concerns and ethics in need based experimentation on animals and plants, would be addressed. Emphasis will also be made on health care related issues.

course_codes.supporting_text: Course No. : BITS F467 / BITS U467

title: Mechanics of Solids
scope: This course aims at providing overall understanding of various methods in understanding the behavior of structural elements under various loading conditions. title: SURVEYING
scope: The course introduces the students to various basic techniques in surveying, viz., chain, compass, theodolite, plane table, tacheometry, traversing, and calculation of areas and volumes, along with fundamentals of a few advanced surveying techniques.
description: The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been included so that the student will be able to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes, which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these areas have also been included.

title: Civil Engineering Materials
scope: The course deals with properties, characterization, testing, selection and quality control of construction material. For economical, durable and high performance of structure, it is imperative to have knowledge on construction materials and their wider applications. This course provides a basic and enhanced overview of various construction materials presently used in practice.
description: Different types of cements, chemical composition, properties and tests, coarse and fine aggregate for concrete, tests on aggregates, grading of aggregates and its effect on concrete properties, chemical and mineral admixtures, properties and tests on fresh and hardened concrete; transportation and placing of concrete, non- destructive testing of concrete, durability of concrete, quality control and acceptance criteria of concrete, Factors in the choice of mix proportions, Proportioning of concrete mixes by various methods – BIS method of mix design; Introduction to special concretes. Manufacturing/sources, classification, applications, properties and testing of bricks, blocks, tiles, aggregates, lime, timber, paints, glass, bitumen, cutback, emulsion, modified bitumen, steel, non-ferrous metals, polymeric materials, geo-synthetics, etc. Low cost and waste material in construction. Latest, BIS, IRC & ASTM specifications and guidelines of all above- mentioned material, and construction equipment.

title: Fluid Mechanics
instructor: Dr. Guntu Ravikumar (M W 5 Th 10 at 6104)
scope: • Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications • Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques • Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces • Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies • Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions • Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems • Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches • Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction • Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles • Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude
description: Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.

source.supporting_text: Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.

scope.supporting_text: • Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications • Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques • Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces • Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies • Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions • Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems • Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches • Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction • Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles • Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude

title: Hydraulic Engineering
description: This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and non- uniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to fluid machinery. 2. Scope & Course Objective: The problems encountered by our society, such as water supply, irrigation, navigation, and water power, resulted in the development of Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulic Engineering. The objective of this course is to equip students with a fundamental understanding of the principles of fluid mechanics as applied to hydraulic systems and structures. The course aims to achieve the following Course Objectives (Teacher's perspective), aligned with the Course Outcomes (COs) (Students’ perspective): 1. To develop an analytical understanding of flow behavior in pipes and channels under varying conditions. 2. To apply fluid mechanics principles in analyzing hydraulic systems, including energy losses and force impacts. 3. To introduce the working principles and performance of fluid machinery relevant to civil engineering. 4. To prepare students for practical problem-solving in the analysis, design, and assessment of water infrastructures of Pipe networks, open channels, and structures submerged in fluid, like bridge piers, dealt with by civil engineers.

title: Foundation Engineering
scope: The main goal of this course is to provide an in-depth understanding regarding different types of foundations. Analysis of foundations and retaining structures (Shallow foundations, pile foundations, machine foundations, retaining walls, slope stability etc.) considering all geotechnical aspects. Emphasis will be given on complete coverage of code of practices for various types of foundations and retaining structures. Geotechnical earthquake engineering, ground improvement techniques, reinforced earth walls and geosynthetics applications increased tremendously therefore given due consideration.
description: General requirement for satisfactory performance of shallow foundations, general, local and punching shear failures, bearing capacity, settlement, tilt and rotation of foundations, proportioning of Shallow Foundations, footings on layered soils and slopes, Deep foundations, capacity of single and group Piles, laterally loaded pile, Earth Pressure theories, Retaining structures, design and checks for stability, Stability of slopes, Introduction to Ground Improvement Techniques and geosynthetics with applications, Introduction to machine foundations for different type of machines, Introduction to geotechnical earthquake engineering and liquefaction of soils, computer applications in foundation design

title: DESIGN OF REINFORCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
scope: In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.
description: Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy, Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams; Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length; Design of beams and slabs for serviceability; Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and bi-axial bending; Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases.
