title: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering
scope: Introduction to in-situ testing, drilling, and sampling, advantages and disadvantages of in-situ testing, and scope of using the test results for direct and indirect design of geotechnical structures. • Learn about SPT, test procedure, SPT corrections, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. • Become familiar with some of the frequently used methods for the design of foundations using SPT data. • Learn about CPT, test procedure, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. • Design of foundations based on CPT results. • Assess liquefaction potential for a site based on SPT and CPT results. • Estimate seismic wave velocities and interpret subsurface profiles based on seismic reflection and refraction tests, and SASW test. • Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs based on exploration findings will be discussed.
description: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results, including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpful to students when they start working as practicing engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering.

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
scope: The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
description: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

title: Fundamentals of Systems Engineering
scope: The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure planning, development, and management. Students will explore systems architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and evidence-based planning.
description: Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation, maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic, systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.

The course also integrates modern tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and evidence-based planning.
description: Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation, maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic, systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.

title: Transportation Systems Planning and Management
scope: The course aims at imparting knowledge on understanding of urban transportation problems in planners’ perspective, definition of the problem, setting clear goals and objectives to serve as guiding factors in the planning process, identification of the causal factors influencing the demand for urban travel and development of relationship between the factors and the travel demand.
description: System and environment; sequential transportation systems planning: trip generation, trip distribution, modal split and traffic assignment, Transportation surveys, Land-use models, Travel demand forecasting, Urban structure and its influence of travel intensity, Urban goods movement. Transportation Systems Management (TSM) actions: traffic management techniques for improving vehicular flow, preferential treatment for high occupancy modes, demand management technique for reduced traffic demand, staggered hours, vehicle restrictions; planning for pedestrians.

title: Water Resources Planning and Management
scope: The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making.
makeup_policy: 1. Make-up will be granted only on genuine reasons. However, prior permission is must. 2. For medical cases, a certificate from the concerned physician of the Medical Centre must be produced. Minimum Clearing/Passing Score Policy of the Course: A student must obtain 30% of the average of the top two performers in the class, or 40% of the median of the class, whichever is lower to clear the course. This shall be considered as the minimum performance criterion to clear/pass the course. If any student gets the marks lower than the prescribed standard mentioned above, he/she will be awarded NC. Attendance Clause As BITS Pilani is a fully residential university with an internal and continuous evaluation system, it is expected that every student demonstrates a high level of responsibility by maintaining 100% attendance in all classes and laboratory sessions. Regular attendance and class participation are integral components of the learning process, and students are expected to appear in all scheduled tests and examinations and complete assigned academic tasks sincerely and on time. While 100% attendance is the expected norm, under no circumstances should a student’s attendance fall below 60% in this course. A student falling short of this minimum attendance requirement shall not be permitted to appear in the comprehensive examination and will be considered as not having cleared the course. Students are therefore advised to remain fully aware of their academic responsibilities and ensure consistent attendance throughout the semester.

source.supporting_text: EC No. Evaluation component Duration Weightage (%) Date, Time and Nature of Venue component 1 Mid semester 90 min. 25 05/10 AN2 OB 2 Project* (Includes term 30 To be announced OB paper and seminar) from time to time Mid-Semester Project 10-15 min for To be Last week of OB Presentation and Report each Project announced October Final Project 15-25 min for To be First week of OB Presentation and Report each Project announced December 3 Class Participation and 10 To be announced OB (Take Home Assignments from time to time Home) 4 Comprehensive 3 Hours 35 03/12 (AN) CB Examination *During the semester, each student will work in a team on a project dealing with water resources planning and management. These projects will deal with some aspect of a real, complex water resources planning and analysis issue of current interest to the world, nation, or a particular State. The projects typically are interdisciplinary and consider such aspects of water resources planning and management as: engineering, law; economics; hydrology, climatology, hydrogeology; environmental health; computer modeling; population growth; land use planning; regional development; or politics. Each group will make an oral presentation of their progress and outcome to the class during Mid-semester presentation and final presentation and submit the reports accordingly. The purposes of the term project are: 1. To enable you to explore in-depth an aspect of the subject of water resources planning and management. 2. To provide experience in the formulation, execution and presentation of an engineering investigation in the area of water resources planning and management. 3. To provide a teamwork experience dealing with the interdisciplinary nature of water resources planning and management. Steps in Carrying out the Project The steps in carrying out the project are: 1. Prepare a proposal in MS Word and email it to the instructor specifying the objective of your project and outlining how you plan to go about executing it. Before beginning your project, you need to prepare a project proposal and submit it to the instructor for approval and feedback. This proposal should be about 1-2 page in length. The instructor will review the proposals and provide comments for the student to revise the proposal for final submittal and approval. The proposal should contain: • Title of the project, • Team members. • Scope, Definition of the problem and Background of the study, • Objectives, • Plan work, • Discussion (preliminary) of the proposed methods of solution of the problem. • Anticipated data needs. • Anticipated problems in carrying out the project. • Assignment of tasks to team members. • Anticipated outcome • A minimum of 5 bibliographic/references citations relevant to your proposed project. 2. Present an oral report in class on the date posted on the class assignment web page. 3. Send a written report (in MS Word) to the instructor on the date posted on the class assignment web page.

source.supporting_text: The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making.

Prepare a proposal in MS Word and email it to the instructor specifying the objective of your project and outlining how you plan to go about executing it. The instructor will review the proposals and provide comments for the student to revise the proposal for final submittal and approval. Present an oral report in class on the date posted on the class assignment web page. 3. Send a written report (in MS Word) to the instructor on the date posted on the class assignment web page.

source.supporting_text: The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making.

title: CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT
description: The course deals with planning techniques, engineering economy, valuation including estimation & costing, system design, construction methodologies ranging from small buildings to large infrastructure projects, construction technologies including recent advancements. Relevant Indian Standard codes of practices will be given emphasis. 2 (a): Scope of the Course: The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of construction planning and management right from the knowledge of various activities till the estimation, costing, valuation, tendering etc., Though this course covers wider infrastructure projects, the primary focus will be on building and road infrastructure. 2(b): Objectives of the course: ➢ To understand the different construction projects and basic objective of project management [Module - I] ➢ To understand the project management techniques (CPM and PERT) [Module - II] ➢ To analyze the various requirements of manpower and other resources [ Module-III] ➢ To analyze the various control methodologies keeping in line with project requirements [Module-IV] ➢ To get exposed to construction contracts and tenders [Module-V] ➢ To estimate the quantity and rate of different building components (including materials) [Module VI] ➢ To discuss the various aspects of valuation of properties [Module VII] ➢ To highlights various aspects of construction quality and safety with case studies [Module VIII] ➢ To understand the best practices of construction management [Module IX] _ Instruction Division 3.Key Learning outcomes: The students will be trained to • Demonstrate a systematic understanding of the function of project management in property, construction, and the project lifecycle; and of the concepts, theories, principles, and techniques associated with construction project management at strategic and operational level. • Critically apply established techniques of analysis and enquiry to construction project management and use judgement to evaluate a range of solutions. • Provide appropriate construction management advice to organizations in order to meet objectives while meeting required standards of ethics and governance. • Demonstrate the skills to manage procedures and processes during the construction project lifecycle. • Understand the legal implications of contract, common, and regulatory law to manage a construction project

Relevant Indian Standard codes of practices will be given emphasis. 2 (a): Scope of the Course: The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of construction planning and management right from the knowledge of various activities till the estimation, costing, valuation, tendering etc., Though this course covers wider infrastructure projects, the primary focus will be on building and road infrastructure. 2(b): Objectives of the course: ➢ To understand the different construction projects and basic objective of project management [Module - I] ➢ To understand the project management techniques (CPM and PERT) [Module - II] ➢ To analyze the various requirements of manpower and other resources [ Module-III] ➢ To analyze the various control methodologies keeping in line with project requirements [Module-IV] ➢ To get exposed to construction contracts and tenders [Module-V] ➢ To estimate the quantity and rate of different building components (including materials) [Module VI] ➢ To discuss the various aspects of valuation of properties [Module VII] ➢ To highlights various aspects of construction quality and safety with case studies [Module VIII] ➢ To understand the best practices of construction management [Module IX] _ Instruction Division 3.Key Learning outcomes: The students will be trained to • Demonstrate a systematic understanding of the function of project management in property, construction, and the project lifecycle; and of the concepts, theories, principles, and techniques associated with construction project management at strategic and operational level. • Critically apply established techniques of analysis and enquiry to construction project management and use judgement to evaluate a range of solutions. • Provide appropriate construction management advice to organizations in order to meet objectives while meeting required standards of ethics and governance. • Demonstrate the skills to manage procedures and processes during the construction project lifecycle. • Understand the legal implications of contract, common, and regulatory law to manage a construction project

title: Pavement Material Characterization
scope: The main objective of this course is to understand the different material components typical in pavement and learn about the importance of the properties of these components for effective functioning of the pavement. In this course, we would also look into the guidelines outlined for testing, specifications and characterization of various material used in pavements (both nationally and internationally). A brief about the ongoing worldwide research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different lectures.
description: [as per the Bulletin] This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification, compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application, chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would be covered along with design example.

title: AIRPORT PLANNING & DESIGN
scope: The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of airport planning and design. This course is expected to provide a broad overview on various topics as mentioned below. ➢ To understand briefly air transport and aviation industry [Module I] ➢ To understand the need to forecast air transport demand [Module II] ➢ To get the overall idea about aircraft and its influence on entire planning [Module III] ➢ To get a comprehensive overview about airport system and master planning [Module IV] ➢ To get an overview about the factors affecting the airport capacity [Module V] ➢ To comprehensively analyze the airside configuration and geometric design [Module VI] ➢ To understand the structural pavement design and airport drainage [Module VII] ➢ To get a quick overview about different visual aids in airport and in airspace [Module VIII] ➢ To acknowledge the importance of maintenance and rehabilitation of pavement [Module IX] ➢ To know the parameters influencing the airport performance including benchmarking [Module X]
description: The course deals with complete planning and design of airports with greater emphasis on planning not restricted to airports, but air transport at large. The course will also touch base on several other connected aspects of air transportation such as forecasting air transport demand, evolution of aircraft and pavements, air transportation business, sustainability aspects etc.,

title: Pavement Failure Evaluation and Rehabilitation
scope: The course includes the determination of causes of failure in flexible and concrete pavement. The different techniques for evaluation and rehabilitation of different types of distresses will be taught to the students. The use of modern equipment’s for structural evaluation of pavement, and design of overlay with the help of data collected by using the equipment will be covered in this course. The accelerated test facilities constructed worldwide and instrumentation used in these test facilities for pavement evaluation will be taught to the students.
description: This course covers topics related to pavement failure, evaluation and rehabilitation such as pavement deterioration, distress and different types of failures, methods of measurement and treatment, use of modern equipment for pavement surface condition measurements, analysis of data, interpretation, Structural deterioration of pavements: causes, effects, methods of treatment, structural evaluation of flexible pavements by rebound deflection method, analysis of data, design of overlay, use of FWD and other methods for evaluation of flexible and rigid pavements and their application, pavement testing under controlled conditions, test track studies, Instrumentation for pavement testing.
makeup_policy: • Make up will be granted only on genuine reasons and will be considered on a case by case basis. However, prior permission is a must. It should follow the official request procedure. No other mode of request shall be entertained. • For medical cases, a certificate from the concerned physician from the Medical Centre must be produced (Subjected to Academic regulations). • Make up policy is only applicable to Mid – Semester test and Comprehensive Examination. It is not applicable to quiz and project presentation.

title: Rural Road Technology
scope: Rural roads are the key components for the development of rural community. In this regard, the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched by the Govt. of India to provide connectivity to unconnected Habitations as part of a poverty reduction strategy. Subsequently, the various strategies have been adopted in planning and construction of rural roads with the aid of technologically advanced construction practices. The scope of the course is to know the various aspects rural roads construction and the various processes associated with the construction. In the recent past, special emphasis is on the use of green technology for road construction in many states. Rural road technology is fast evolving at an urban pace. The course aims to cover various technological advancements that have taken place not only in India, but also on the global stage.
description: Network planning, accessibility and mobility; road alignment and survey; geometric design: cross sectional elements, sight distance, horizontal and vertical alignments; road materials and use of marginal materials; pavement design, drainage, culverts and small bridges; construction and specifications; quality control in construction; pavement failures; maintenance; preparation of detailed project report (DPR); community participation in planning, design, construction and management.

title: DYNAMICS OF STRUCTURES
scope: Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on this scope, the following objectives have been listed:  To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/ industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure, tall chimneys etc.  To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.
description: Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures; origins of vibration theory and experiment; review of earlier concepts: D’Alembert’s principle, equations of motion. Elements of a structural system: springs, dashpot, mass; Springs in parallel and series; methods to formulate equations of motion; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped free vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Forced vibration under harmonic, periodic, impulse, step, ramp, general dynamic forces (time and frequency domain analysis) and response spectrum load, support excited vibration, seismic pickups; Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response of SDOF system; time domain analysis; direct integration techniques; finite difference method (Central Difference method); Newmark beta method; average and linear acceleration method; Development of equation of motion and solution for two degree of freedom systems; Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems; frequencies; mode shapes and response; orthogonality condition of mode shapes; Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes; Holzer method; Stodola’s method; Rayleigh’s method; Rayleigh-Ritz method; Inverse iteration method; Vector iteration method; Rayleigh’s Quotient iteration method; Matrix iteration method; Generation of damping matrix for MDOF; dynamic properties; modal damping; classical damping; damped response with Rayleigh and Caughey damping.Mode superposition method; mode acceleration method; modal combination rules using absolute sum, SRSS and CQC method.

scope.supporting_text: Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on this scope, the following objectives have been listed:  To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/ industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure, tall chimneys etc.  To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.

description.supporting_text: Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures; origins of vibration theory and experiment; review of earlier concepts: D’Alembert’s principle, equations of motion. Elements of a structural system: springs, dashpot, mass; Springs in parallel and series; methods to formulate equations of motion; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped free vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Forced vibration under harmonic, periodic, impulse, step, ramp, general dynamic forces (time and frequency domain analysis) and response spectrum load, support excited vibration, seismic pickups; Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response of SDOF system; time domain analysis; direct integration techniques; finite difference method (Central Difference method); Newmark beta method; average and linear acceleration method; Development of equation of motion and solution for two degree of freedom systems; Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems; frequencies; mode shapes and response; orthogonality condition of mode shapes; Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes; Holzer method; Stodola’s method; Rayleigh’s method; Rayleigh-Ritz method; Inverse iteration method; Vector iteration method; Rayleigh’s Quotient iteration method; Matrix iteration method; Generation of damping matrix for MDOF; dynamic properties; modal damping; classical damping; damped response with Rayleigh and Caughey damping.Mode superposition method; mode acceleration method; modal combination rules using absolute sum, SRSS and CQC method.

title: ADVANCED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
scope: The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind & earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins, nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete. Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding. ➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I] ➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II] ➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III] ➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV] ➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V] ➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI] ➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII] ➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII] ➢ To discuss the case studies of different RC structures and its failures [Module IX] ➢ To discuss the various advancements in concrete structures and the research scope [Module X]
description: The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design of various elements and exposure to different code provisions. Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall buildings, detailing in concrete structures

scope.supporting_text: The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind & earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins, nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete. Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding. ➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I] ➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II] ➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III] ➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV] ➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V] ➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI] ➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII] ➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII] ➢ To discuss the case studies of different RC structures and its failures [Module IX] ➢ To discuss the various advancements in concrete structures and the research scope [Module X]

description.supporting_text: The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design of various elements and exposure to different code provisions. Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall buildings, detailing in concrete structures

title: PRESTRESSED CONCRETE STRUCTURES
scope: The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications. The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of practicing structural design engineers. The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members. This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed concrete structures.
description: Introduction to basic concepts of prestressing; prestressing systems; analysis of prestress; losses in prestress; deflection; design of anchorage zone, design of prestressed concrete girders.

source.supporting_text: The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications. The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of practicing structural design engineers. The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members. This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed concrete structures.

title: BRIDGE ENGINEERING
scope: Bridges are an inseparable part of any communication network as they are the key elements in roadways and highway networks. This course intends to impart skills for analysis & design of various types of bridges. This course will mainly focus on the design of three types of bridge superstructures namely Slab culverts/bridges, T-beam bridges, and Composite bridges. The design of the bridge substructure will include the design of elastomeric bearings and the design of abutments and piers. Moreover, the course will include the design aspects of continuous bridges. At the end of this course, the students would be equipped with the complete analysis and design of slab, T-beam and composite bridges, along with the design of substructures for them.
description: Purpose of bridge; Classification of bridges; Characteristics of different types of bridges; Loads stresses and their combinations; Design of RCC Slab culverts, Box-culverts, T-beam bridges; composite bridges; continuous bridges; design of bearings; design of piers and abutments and their foundations.
makeup_policy: Make-up will be granted only to genuine cases. For cases related to illness, proper documentary evidence is essential. Prior permission is necessary if a student is out of station on the test date.

title: Advance Structural Analysis
scope: Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using computer oriented approach. The basic objective of this course is to acquire the fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures. By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized
description: [as per the Bulletin] Flexibility Method; stiffness method; beam curved in plan; two dimensional and three dimensional analysis of structures; shear deformations, shear wall analysis; interactive software development for analysis of structures.

scope.supporting_text: Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using computer oriented approach. The basic objective of this course is to acquire the fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures. By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized

description.supporting_text: [as per the Bulletin] Flexibility Method; stiffness method; beam curved in plan; two dimensional and three dimensional analysis of structures; shear deformations, shear wall analysis; interactive software development for analysis of structures.

title: Finite Element Analysis
scope: Finite element method is the most powerful numerical method widely used for solving problems in different branches of engineering especially Civil Engineering. This method is usually used to solve complex problems with regard to complexity in material, geometry, boundary, and loading conditions, such as non-homogeneous material, irregular geometry, boundary conditions, and static & dynamic loading conditions. The finite element formulation from the weak form of the governing differential equations is also covered. The course is aimed to enable students to understand the advanced concept of finite element method and its application to Civil Engineering.
description: Fundamentals of the finite element method (FEM); basic formulations of FEM; steps in FEM; 1-D, 2- D and 3-D elements; axi-symmetric elements, isoparametric formulations; programming aspects in FEM; plate bending elements; shell elements; material and geometric nonlinearity; Buckling and Vibration problems, application of FEM to civil engineering problems.

title: Environmental Impact Assessment
scope: The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.
description: Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

title: Chemical Process Calculations
scope: This course provides an introduction to the basic fundamentals of chemical engineering. It deals with calculations, which form the basis of the design of a chemical industrial plant or process. It aims to inculcate conceptual knowledge as well as systematic and sound problem solving skills in the student. The concept of material and energy balances are introduced, explained, and worked with the help of examples from the real world chemical process plants. Fundamentals of this course would be required for other courses like Chemical Process Technology, Chemical Reaction Engineering, Separation Processes and Process Modelling and Simulation.
description: Historical overview of Chemical Engineering, Principles of balancing with examples to illustrate differential and integral balances lumped and distributed balances, Material balances in simple systems involving physical changes and chemical reactions, Systems involving recycle, purge and bypass, Properties of substances: single component & multicomponent, single and multiphase systems. Ideal liquid and gaseous mixtures, Energy balance calculations in simple systems, Introduction to Computer aided calculations-steady state material and energy balances for chemical plants

title: Fluid Mechanics
scope: This course is an introduction to the field of fluid mechanics. It mainly covers the basic principles of fluid mechanics. It introduces the student to the fundamental and practical aspects of fluid flow operations that a practising chemical engineer encounters regularly. The physical concepts of fluid mechanics and analysis methods, beginning from basic principles, shall be dealt with in this course.
description: Fundamental Concepts, Fluid Statics, Integral and Differential Analysis for Fluid Motion, Dimensional Analysis, Internal and External Fluid Flow, Fluid Machinery, Flow through Packed Bed, Agitation, Introduction to Compressible Flow.

scope.supporting_text: This course is an introduction to the field of fluid mechanics. It mainly covers the basic principles of fluid mechanics. It introduces the student to the fundamental and practical aspects of fluid flow operations that a practising chemical engineer encounters regularly. The physical concepts of fluid mechanics and analysis methods, beginning from basic principles, shall be dealt with in this course.

description.supporting_text: Fundamental Concepts, Fluid Statics, Integral and Differential Analysis for Fluid Motion, Dimensional Analysis, Internal and External Fluid Flow, Fluid Machinery, Flow through Packed Bed, Agitation, Introduction to Compressible Flow.

title: Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics
scope:  Understanding laws of thermodynamics and applying the concept for heat, work and energy calculations.  Analyze essential conditions (temperature, pressure, composition, etc.) for simple physical and chemical changes.  Thermodynamic properties calculation for ideal and real fluids.  Apply thermodynamic principles in estimation/calculation of thermodynamic efficiency  Application of thermodynamic principals for understanding the criterion (G, equilibria constant, etc.) of simple chemical reaction at equilibria, degree of conversion, composition and effect of P, inert gas addition, excess reactants, products on conversion, etc.  VLE calculations for phase-equilibria. 3. Students learning outcomes: 1. Develop ability to analyze heat, energy, and work requirement/transfer for simple physical and chemical processes using laws of thermodynamics. 2. Applying principles of thermodynamics to chemical engineering systems. 3. Industrial design of reactors, separators and utilities using principles of thermodynamics. 4. Thermodynamic efficiency calculation for chemical engineering processes. 5. Feasibility of chemical engineering processes based on thermodynamic properties calculations.
description: Applications of first and second laws; relations between state properties; chemical equilibria in reacting and non-reacting systems; statistical concepts, and brief exposure to irreversible thermodynamics; extensive problem assignments throughout. [Review of work, heat, reversible and irreversible processes, First Law applications to closed and open systems, Second Law, Entropy, Heat effects, Equations of state and generalized correlations for PVT behavior, Maxwell relations and fluid properties estimation; Residual and excess properties, Partial molar quantities; Gibbs-Duhem Equation, Fugacity and Activity Coefficient models, Vapor-Liquid equilibria, chemical reaction equilibrium.

title: Engineering Chemistry
scope: The course aims to introduce various aspects of chemistry as applied to engineering. The course also aims to bridge the theoretical concepts and their practical engineering applications, thus highlighting the role of chemistry in the field of chemical engineering.
description: Introduction to basic principles of various branches of chemistry and their applications in chemical Industries. Organic chemistry (Important functional groups and their reactions, Some important name reactions commonly used in the chemical industry); Physical chemistry (Thermodynamic processes, Thermochemistry, Electrochemistry, Adsorption, Catalysis), Chemical methods of analysis (volumetric analysis: neutralization, redox, complexometric titrations), Instrumental methods of analysis ( IR, UV- vis spectroscopy, Chromatography), Engineering materials (cementing materials, refractories, polymers), Metals and alloys (Iron and steel), Corrosion (types of corrosion and corrosion control methods), Water treatment (Hardness of water, water analysis and water treatment), Fuels and combustion (Classification of fuels, Analysis of coal, Combustion, Calorific value and its determination).

In case of out of campus medical consultation, the CMO of BITS Medical Center must certify the authenticity of your document and issue you a certificate on their official letter head. Except for emergency situations, prior permission of IC is compulsory. No makeup will be granted for evaluative components with a buffer. 12. AI Based Term Project: The students will be divided into a group of 3-4 students per team. Each team will be required to develop an AI based project on engineering chemistry applications. A few project titles are listed here but a team will be free to propose any project relevant to the course. The proposed project must be approved by the I/C prior to the initiation.  Predicting Water Quality Parameters Using Machine Learning  Spectral Data Classification Using AI  AI-Based Fuel Quality Estimation  Predicting Corrosion Risk Based on Environmental Factors  Polymer Property Prediction Using Molecular Descriptors  Reaction Condition Optimization Using AI

title: Kinetics & Reactor Design (KRD)
scope: This course is an introduction to the chemical reaction kinetics, design and performance of various types of chemical reactors for chemically reacting systems, which yield industrially important products. The emphasis in this course will be to understand the fundamentals of kinetics of homogeneous reactions, design and analysis of ideal reactors; and non-ideal flow.
description: Kinetics Reaction rate, order, rate constant; Batch reactors Design + basics; Kinetic constants from batch reactor data; Ideal flow reactors Mass and Energy balances; Isothermal, adiabatic and non-isothermal operation; Catalysts, Catalytic rates, Reaction mechanisms; Internal/External transport in catalysts; Non-catalytic solid-gas reactions; Reactor design for ideal flow reactors; Kinetics of Solid Catalyzed Reactions; Yield and Selectivity; Concept of RTD; Segregation and Maximum Mixedness models.

scope.supporting_text: This course is an introduction to the chemical reaction kinetics, design and performance of various types of chemical reactors for chemically reacting systems, which yield industrially important products. The emphasis in this course will be to understand the fundamentals of kinetics of homogeneous reactions, design and analysis of ideal reactors; and non-ideal flow.

description.supporting_text: Kinetics Reaction rate, order, rate constant; Batch reactors Design + basics; Kinetic constants from batch reactor data; Ideal flow reactors Mass and Energy balances; Isothermal, adiabatic and non-isothermal operation; Catalysts, Catalytic rates, Reaction mechanisms; Internal/External transport in catalysts; Non-catalytic solid-gas reactions; Reactor design for ideal flow reactors; Kinetics of Solid Catalyzed Reactions; Yield and Selectivity; Concept of RTD; Segregation and Maximum Mixedness models.

title: Chemical Engineering Laboratory -1
scope: The main objective of this course is to familiarize the students on different principles of chemical engineering through hands on experimentation. The experiments are designed to enable students to apply the theoretical background assimilated in the relevant chemical engineering courses to practice in a laboratory environment. Emphasis is laid on employing scientific methodology in practice: each experiment requires planning, data collection, calculations based on chemical engineering principles, critical analysis, discussion and presentation of the observed result. Additionally, the students will also learn the operation of laboratory scale scientific equipment.
description: The course comprises of experiments in three major areas of chemical engineering, i.e., fluid mechanics, heattransfer and mass transfer. The course involves experiments designed to cover the areas related to the theory of 1. Fluid flow: flow through packed and fluidized beds, major and minor losses associated with fluid flow,flow characteristics, continuity principle, boundary layer theory and fluid moving machinery, 2. Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation and heat exchange equipments such as heat exchangers (shell and tube, double pipe, plate type, finned tube) and condensers. 3. Mass transfer: Vapor liquid equilibrium (VLE), separation based on volatility, mass transfer equipments such as distillation column, packed bed adsorber, and mass transfer with reaction and other relevant concepts.
makeup_policy: As mentioned above, make-up for selected evaluative components will be granted for genuine cases only with proper documentation. For all such cases, prior permission of the I/C is compulsory. Decision of the I/C will be final in all the cases.

Description of Evaluative Components and Associated Policies: 9.1 Lab Report: Guideline for Laboratory Report Submission ● At the beginning of the semester, all students will be encouraged to form a group of 3 or 4 amongst themselves. Please note that due to operational constraints, a group size smaller or larger than prescribed may not be feasible. ● On the day of conduction of the lab experiment, a datasheet with experimental results will be noted by each group member. Based on the observation sheets, the students will compile a report which should include the following:- ○ Aim & Objectives of the experiment: 1 mark ○ Laboratory Observations: 1 mark ○ Sample Calculations: 2 marks ○ Results and Discussion: 1 marks ○ Conclusions and Understanding: 1 mark ● Students are encouraged to utilize the lab hours for carrying out sample calculations, data visualization and building insights for the discussion part of the lab report, particularly since both faculty and TAs are available live during this time to solve your doubts on spot. ● It’s expected that every group will submit a lab report as a hardcopy (printout) at the lab and attach it to a master file maintained at the lab for this purpose. Please make sure you write name and ID of all group members on top of each page. You are free to use any platforms/software for report generation,data analysis and visualization. Use of technology is encouraged. Handwritten and scanned reports won’t be accepted! ● The students are encouraged to work along with their groupmates to draft the report. However, the “Conclusions and Understanding” section of the report needs to be individually written by each group member. This means that each report will have 3 or 4 separate conclusion and understanding (i.e., one by each student in the group) ● Lab report will be due one week after the completion of the experiment. Only those lab reports which are received on the due date will be evaluated. ● Plagiarism: As highlighted, you’re requested to submit a professional quality digitally printed lab report. Plagiarism might be construed as academic dishonesty and your submitted lab reports may be subjected through plagiarism detection software(s). While we understand there might be a few technical phrases common in all the lab reports, hence there won’t be any penalty for similarity up-to 20%. However, there would be 50% marks deduction for those whose reports are 20%-40% similar. If found more than 40% similarity, zero marks will be awarded for involved students. Decision of I/C will be final in all such cases. 9.2 Cylce-1/Cycle-2 Lab Exam:  The mid/end sem lab exam will be a closed book lab exam, where the students will perform experiments at the lab on their own and submit a report in the designated time slot.  The students will be asked to pick an experiment (through lucky draw) from a pool of experiments relevant to their cycle.  A handwritten report (similar to the lab report) needs to be written and submitted for evaluation in given time slot.  The experiments will be shortened to enable timely completion of the experiment and report writing.  No separate make-up for the Lab Exams will be allowed. 9.3 Comprehensive Quiz: 9.3.1 A comprehensive quiz will be conducted on the designated date as a closed book exam. Questions and options (in case of multiple choice questions) would be randomized and it’s in your best interest to focus on your questions in hand since the time would be limited. 9.3.2 The quiz will be based on the theory behind the experiments covered in the lab and may include question on concepts pertaining to the chemical engineering principles involved in the experiments. 9.3.3 No separate make-up for the quiz will be allowed. 9.4 Comprehensive Viva-voce Examination: 9.4.1 Viva will be closed book and you will be tested on clarity of concepts related to the experiments conducted, background theory, experimental procedure, calculations, data analysis and applications. 9.4.2 A panel of all instructors will take the viva and give individual marks. Average of those marks would then be taken and communicated to you. Please note that we may not be able to give you individual break-up of marks in viva. 9.4.3 Only genuine requests for viva make-up backed by paperwork/evidence/proof will be entertained. A prior email permission would be necessary. Decision of the I/C will be final in all such cases. 10. Online Consultation Hour: will be announced during the orientation.

Based on the observation sheets, the students will compile a report which should include the following:- ○ Aim & Objectives of the experiment: 1 mark ○ Laboratory Observations: 1 mark ○ Sample Calculations: 2 marks ○ Results and Discussion: 1 marks ○ Conclusions and Understanding: 1 mark ● Students are encouraged to utilize the lab hours for carrying out sample calculations, data visualization and building insights for the discussion part of the lab report, particularly since both faculty and TAs are available live during this time to solve your doubts on spot. ● It’s expected that every group will submit a lab report as a hardcopy (printout) at the lab and attach it to a master file maintained at the lab for this purpose. Please make sure you write name and ID of all group members on top of each page. You are free to use any platforms/software for report generation,data analysis and visualization. Use of technology is encouraged. Handwritten and scanned reports won’t be accepted! ● The students are encouraged to work along with their groupmates to draft the report. However, the “Conclusions and Understanding” section of the report needs to be individually written by each group member. This means that each report will have 3 or 4 separate conclusion and understanding (i.e., one by each student in the group) ● Lab report will be due one week after the completion of the experiment. Only those lab reports which are received on the due date will be evaluated. ● Plagiarism: As highlighted, you’re requested to submit a professional quality digitally printed lab report. Plagiarism might be construed as academic dishonesty and your submitted lab reports may be subjected through plagiarism detection software(s). While we understand there might be a few technical phrases common in all the lab reports, hence there won’t be any penalty for similarity up-to 20%. However, there would be 50% marks deduction for those whose reports are 20%-40% similar. If found more than 40% similarity, zero marks will be awarded for involved students. Decision of I/C will be final in all such cases. 9.2 Cylce-1/Cycle-2 Lab Exam:  The mid/end sem lab exam will be a closed book lab exam, where the students will perform experiments at the lab on their own and submit a report in the designated time slot.  The students will be asked to pick an experiment (through lucky draw) from a pool of experiments relevant to their cycle.  A handwritten report (similar to the lab report) needs to be written and submitted for evaluation in given time slot.  The experiments will be shortened to enable timely completion of the experiment and report writing.  No separate make-up for the Lab Exams will be allowed. 9.3 Comprehensive Quiz: 9.3.1 A comprehensive quiz will be conducted on the designated date as a closed book exam. Questions and options (in case of multiple choice questions) would be randomized and it’s in your best interest to focus on your questions in hand since the time would be limited. 9.3.2 The quiz will be based on the theory behind the experiments covered in the lab and may include question on concepts pertaining to the chemical engineering principles involved in the experiments. 9.3.3 No separate make-up for the quiz will be allowed. 9.4 Comprehensive Viva-voce Examination: 9.4.1 Viva will be closed book and you will be tested on clarity of concepts related to the experiments conducted, background theory, experimental procedure, calculations, data analysis and applications. 9.4.2 A panel of all instructors will take the viva and give individual marks. Average of those marks would then be taken and communicated to you. Please note that we may not be able to give you individual break-up of marks in viva. 9.4.3 Only genuine requests for viva make-up backed by paperwork/evidence/proof will be entertained. A prior email permission would be necessary. Decision of the I/C will be final in all such cases. 10. Online Consultation Hour: will be announced during the orientation.

scope.supporting_text: The main objective of this course is to familiarize the students on different principles of chemical engineering through hands on experimentation. The experiments are designed to enable students to apply the theoretical background assimilated in the relevant chemical engineering courses to practice in a laboratory environment. Emphasis is laid on employing scientific methodology in practice: each experiment requires planning, data collection, calculations based on chemical engineering principles, critical analysis, discussion and presentation of the observed result. Additionally, the students will also learn the operation of laboratory scale scientific equipment.

description.supporting_text: The course comprises of experiments in three major areas of chemical engineering, i.e., fluid mechanics, heattransfer and mass transfer. The course involves experiments designed to cover the areas related to the theory of 1. Fluid flow: flow through packed and fluidized beds, major and minor losses associated with fluid flow,flow characteristics, continuity principle, boundary layer theory and fluid moving machinery, 2. Heat transfer: conduction, convection, radiation and heat exchange equipments such as heat exchangers (shell and tube, double pipe, plate type, finned tube) and condensers. 3. Mass transfer: Vapor liquid equilibrium (VLE), separation based on volatility, mass transfer equipments such as distillation column, packed bed adsorber, and mass transfer with reaction and other relevant concepts.

title: Separation Processes II
scope: This course gives the basic understanding of Mechanical Operations, which involves size reduction, size separation, filtration, etc. and certain Mass Transfer Operations like humidification, drying, adsorption, membrane separation, and crystallization. It covers the fundamentals, application of each of these unit operations and the equipment used is discussed in detail. The objective of the course is to orient the students to the industrial practices, which involve both mechanical operations and mass transfer operations, so that they can understand them better.
description: Special equilibrium-based separations like humidification and water cooling, drying of wet solids, adsorption, crystallization etc., Mechanical separations like filtration, centrifugation, froth floatation etc., Solid separations based on size reduction including sieving operations and related equipment like crushers, mills, pulverizers etc., special separation processes like ion-exchange, membranes, chromatography etc.

scope.supporting_text: This course gives the basic understanding of Mechanical Operations, which involves size reduction, size separation, filtration, etc. and certain Mass Transfer Operations like humidification, drying, adsorption, membrane separation, and crystallization. It covers the fundamentals, application of each of these unit operations and the equipment used is discussed in detail. The objective of the course is to orient the students to the industrial practices, which involve both mechanical operations and mass transfer operations, so that they can understand them better.

description.supporting_text: Special equilibrium-based separations like humidification and water cooling, drying of wet solids, adsorption, crystallization etc., Mechanical separations like filtration, centrifugation, froth floatation etc., Solid separations based on size reduction including sieving operations and related equipment like crushers, mills, pulverizers etc., special separation processes like ion-exchange, membranes, chromatography etc.

title: Process Design Principles I
scope: This course introduces the student to process engineering and provides an insight into various aspects of process design. This course mainly deals with the process synthesis part of process design. It covers in detail the preliminary process synthesis, developing base case design, and using heuristics to choose the best from various process alternatives.
description: Process invention using heuristics and analysis (The Design process, Process creation and heuristics for process synthesis, Role of process simulators like Aspen Plus in process creation), Strategic designs in process synthesis and analysis, Detailed process synthesis using algorithmic methods with emphasis on reactor networks, separation trains, batch processes, heat and mass integration, energy integration analysis; pinch technology.
makeup_policy: No make-up will be granted for quizzes (Class + ASPEN-HYSYS). Make-up for Mid Semester Test and Comprehensive Examination will be granted only for genuine reason(s) for not appearing in the regular test. Proper proofs must be submitted along with Make-up application. Prior permission of IC is compulsory.

title: Environmental Pollution Control
scope: 1. Students will learn significance of environmental engineering course, effect of greenhouse effect on climate change, river pollution etc. 2. They will know theoretically how to do air pollutants sampling & Analysis of Air Pollutants 3. They understand basic modelling techniques of the dispersion of the pollutant in air. 4. They will learn basic designing aspects of different methods and equipment for air pollution control. 5. Students will gather idea on sources & classification of water pollutants: Origin of wastewater, their effects, Dissolved oxygen estimation, etc. 6. They learn how to collect wastewater samples and analyse: Understanding and analysis of concepts of DO, BOD, COD, TOC, Water Quality Standards, etc. 7. They comprehend the basics of wastewater treatment methods, biological treatments, Tertiary treatments, Zone settling process & technology 8. Students will learn Sources and Classification of solid wastes, Methods of Collection, Disposal methods , different Hazardous Wastes, treatment and managements, etc. 9. In Module 9 they will explore sources of noise, effects, measurement of noise, control techniques, etc.
description: Air & water pollutants; sampling and analysis; control methods for air & water pollutants; modeling of different control techniques; advanced wastewater treatment processes; solid waste management, noise pollution; case studies; associated laboratory.

title: MOLECULAR AND STATISTICAL THERMODYNAMICS
scope: The objective of the course is to introduce the students with the microscopic description of the thermodynamics system and how macroscopic properties can be derived from microscopic description using statistical mechanics or statistical thermodynamics. In this course the statistical ensembles in classical mechanics, the concept of ensemble and phase space will help in understanding equilibrium statistical mechanics. Beyond this, this course will introduce the coding in either MATLAB or Python to do statistical analysis to find the thermodynamic or dynamic properties of the system. Several simulation techniques such as Monte Carlo Simulations and Molecular Dynamics using GROMACS will be introduced to study applications of statistical thermodynamics to calculate various properties at nanoscale. • Course learning outcomes: a. Learning the fundamental concept of Statistical Thermodynamics b. Learning the concept of molecular dynamics simulation and Monte Carlo Simulation c. Learning the GROMACS and LAMMPS software to perform
description: Fundamental of Statistical Mechanics, Postulates, Concept of Ensembles, statistical interpretation of entropy. Intermolecular Potential Energy functions; Distribution functions: Radial Distribution Function (RDF); Applications of Statistical Mechanics: Thermo-physical property calculations in ensembles; Cooperative Phenomenon: Phase Equilibria: Ising model, Gibbs Ensemble (VLE), Thermodynamic Integration, Gibbs- Duhem Integration, Free Energy calculation; Virial EOS: second virial coefficient; Special Applications: From Surface Adsorption: Adsorption Isotherm. Molecular Simulation Techniques: Molecular Dynamics and Monte Carlo Simulation, Monte Carlo Simulation in various Ensemble.

title: Atomic and Molecular Simulations
scope: This course aims to give an overall introduction to various types of particle-based simulation techniques in the sub-micro level phenomena with hands-on training. Currently, with the advances in computational tools, more and more industries/researchers are focusing on using computational tools to study material properties for various applications. The course will include computational multi-scale methods, from first principle ab initio calculations to molecular mechanics, offering potential pathways for studying advanced materials for several applications such as molecular electronics, energy storage/generation, separation, and purification, to name a few. After successful completion of the course, the students will be equipped with the theoretical basis and algorithms of several atomic and molecular simulations techniques (DFT, MD, MC) with their typical application areas and will be able to solve real- world problems by choosing the right simulation techniques.
description: This course is to equip students with the knowledge of a variety of modern simulation methods at the atomic and molecular levels. The course will deal with several atomic and molecular simulation methods e.g., ab initio methods, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Monte Carlo (MC) methods, free energy algorithms, coarse-graining, and multiscale methods. The course will provide hands-on training for simulations using GROMACS or LAMMPS or similar and hands-on simulations using any DFT packages such as VASP, Quantum Espresso or similar. The course also introduces concepts and algorithms based on programming languages (e.g., Matlab, C, C++, Molecular Modelling Software, and Visual Software). Case studies and examples of several real-life applications will be presented for all the simulation techniques.

source.supporting_text: This course aims to give an overall introduction to various types of particle-based simulation techniques in the sub-micro level phenomena with hands-on training. Currently, with the advances in computational tools, more and more industries/researchers are focusing on using computational tools to study material properties for various applications. The course will include computational multi-scale methods, from first principle ab initio calculations to molecular mechanics, offering potential pathways for studying advanced materials for several applications such as molecular electronics, energy storage/generation, separation, and purification, to name a few. After successful completion of the course, the students will be equipped with the theoretical basis and algorithms of several atomic and molecular simulations techniques (DFT, MD, MC) with their typical application areas and will be able to solve real- world problems by choosing the right simulation techniques.

description.supporting_text: This course is to equip students with the knowledge of a variety of modern simulation methods at the atomic and molecular levels. The course will deal with several atomic and molecular simulation methods e.g., ab initio methods, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Monte Carlo (MC) methods, free energy algorithms, coarse-graining, and multiscale methods. The course will provide hands-on training for simulations using GROMACS or LAMMPS or similar and hands-on simulations using any DFT packages such as VASP, Quantum Espresso or similar. The course also introduces concepts and algorithms based on programming languages (e.g., Matlab, C, C++, Molecular Modelling Software, and Visual Software). Case studies and examples of several real-life applications will be presented for all the simulation techniques.

title: Advanced Transport Phenomena | ATP
scope: Transport phenomena is one of the basic subjects of chemical engineering and includes study of fluid dynamics, heat and mass transfer. The governing equations for the aforementioned transport processes are analogous in nature as the underlying molecular mechanisms are very closely related. The objective of this course is to cover advance topics in this area like the transport of momentum, heat and mass in turbulent flow, creeping flows, flow through porous media, flow over flat plates and curved surfaces, interphase transport, etc. A balanced overview and fundamental equations for transport processes would be provided along with illustrations regarding solving relevant problems. Further, some special cases which are frequently encountered would also be covered.
description: Viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity, Shell momentum and energy balance, equations of change for isothermal and non-isothermal systems, Concentration distribution in solids and laminar flows, momentum, thermal and concentration boundary layers near walls, origin of turbulence, length scales in turbulent flows, Reynolds (RANS) equations, estimates of Reynolds stress (k-epsilon and k-omega type models), turbulent shear flow near a wall, turbulent flow in pipes and channels, turbulent heat transfer, Introduction to large eddy simulations models, rheology and material functions, non-Newtonian viscosity and generalized Newtonian models, Linear and non-linear visco-elasticity, radiation heat transfer, multi-component systems, Coupled heat and mass transfer, evaporation, boiling and condensation, chemical reactions, Special topics: Flow through porous media, compressible flows, multiphase flow, Transport phenomena in biochemical systems.
