title: Communication Systems
scope: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.
description: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization

title: Electromagnetic Fields and Microwave Engineering
scope: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonators, and dielectric structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S-parameters, impedance matching techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators, amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristics. The objective is to equip students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications.
description: Review of Maxwell's equations; Wave propagation: Normal & Oblique incidence; Transmission Lines & Smith Chart, Waveguide: Rectangular & Cylindrical waveguides; Dielectric Waveguides; Cavity resonator, equivalent Circuit Model, characteristics; Microwave devices (Waveguide based and planar); S parameters; Measurement & Impedance Matching; Microwave Generators & Amplifiers; Antennas and its characteristics and types.

course_codes.supporting_text: Course No. : EEE / INSTR/ECE F376, F377

title: Digital Signal Processing
scope: a) To provide a comprehensive knowledge of DSP's fundamental theory, concepts, and applications. b) To be able to design and simulate practical DSP-based systems, finding applications in various fields, namely, communication engineering, audio, video, and image signal processing.
description: Introduction; design of analog filters; design of digital filters (IIR and FIR); structures for the realization of digital filters; random signals and random processes; linear estimation and prediction; Wiener filters; DSP processor architecture; DSP algorithms for different applications.

title: PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS
scope: The main objective is to introduce the fundamental concepts and tools necessary to acquire an understanding of economic decision making of market participants such as Individual households, firms, and the government. The course covers two major areas of economics namely Microeconomics and Macroeconomics. The knowledge of the fundamentals would help the students to better understand the entire economic system and the process followed in policy making. This course would lay foundation for the students to understand other related courses in economics & finance such as Mathematical Economics, International Economics, Advance Micro and Macroeconomics, among others.
description: This course is a foundation course for the students entering into the discipline of Economics & Finance. This introductory course teaches the basic concepts related to the economic system that are listed as follows: Introduction to Economics (Microeconomics) & Economic Problems; Demand, Supply, & Elasticity; Household Behavior and Consumer choice; The Production Process; Costs and Output Decisions; Demand for Production Inputs; Market Imperfections: Monopoly, Oligopoly, Monopolistic Competition; Introduction to Macroeconomics and the Problems; Measurement of National Income & Output; Money Supply and the Banking System

title: [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]
scope: The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.
description: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.

The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.

description.supporting_text: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.

title: MATHEMATICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS
scope: The main objective is to learn how to use mathematical and statistical methods in economics. It involves a review of the fundamentals of mathematics and statistics, which can be used in applied economics. Knowledge of these fundamentals and their application in applied economics would help students better understand the entire economic system and the policymaking process. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand and solve graduate-level problems in economics and finance using the knowledge they have gained. Specifically, this course uses fundamentals from calculus, algebra, optimization, and basic statistics. This course would lay the foundation for students to understand related courses in economics and finance, such as econometrics and growth theory.
description: The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of various statistical and mathematical methods useful for decision-making and for understanding applications in other economics and finance courses. The course is divided into two parts: Statistical Methods and Mathematical Methods. Statistical Methods include methods of collecting and describing statistical data – types of data and data collection methodologies, sampling methods & design, data describing methods (graphical and numerical); Correlation and Regression analyses; Index numbers: Concepts, uses, and methods of construction; Analysis of Time-series: Components, data generating process, and stationarity; Statistical Inference: Introduction to Probability and its distributions, sampling distributions, theory of estimation, Tests of Hypotheses testing (Parametric & Non-Parametric); and Mathematical Methods include Concepts from Linear Algebra & their Applications (Matrices, Input-Output analysis, and Game Theory); Concepts from Calculus and their applications; Introduction to Optimization in Economics and its Applications.

title: ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS
scope: The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context. 3. Learning Outcome of the Course: This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically.
description: Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure.

scope.supporting_text: The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context. 3. Learning Outcome of the Course: This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically.

description.supporting_text: Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure.

title: INTERNATIONAL ECONOMICS
scope:  To understand the effects of international trade on individuals and businesses  To understand the effects of changes in trade policies on trade  To apply macroeconomic models to understand the international economy.  To focus on the interrelationships among aggregate economic variables such as GDP, unemployment rates, inflation rates, trade balances, exchange rates, interest rates, etc.  To focus on the significance of trade imbalances, the determinants of exchange rates, and the aggregate effects of government monetary and fiscal policies.
description: This course develops a systematic exposition of both classical and modern theories of international trade in goods and services that try to explain the composition, direction, and consequences of international trade, and the determinants and effects of trade policy. The course will look critically at the welfare and profit implications of trade policy deviations from free trade. It then builds on the models of open economy macroeconomics.

title: ISSUES IN ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
scope: The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real- world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. Pilani | Dubai | Goa | Hyderabad ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION
description: This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long- run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.

scope.supporting_text: The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real- world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. description.supporting_text: This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long- run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.

title: Financial Management
scope: This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel.
description: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.

title: Derivatives & Risk Management
scope: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA).

title: BUSINESS ANALYSIS AND VALUATION
scope: The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions. 3. Expected Learning Outcome of the Course: The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of financial analysis, advanced accounting practices, and valuation techniques. By the end of the program, learners will be able to effectively analyze financial statements, gaining insights into an organization's performance and financial health. A critical component of the curriculum focuses on valuation methods, where students will learn to assess the value of assets and investments using various approaches, such as discounted cash flow analysis and market comparables. This knowledge will empower them to evaluate investment opportunities critically and make informed decisions that can significantly impact an organization's financial strategy. Overall, these outcomes will prepare students for successful careers in finance and accounting, equipping them with both analytical and practical skills essential for navigating complex financial landscapes.
description: This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements, assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking in business valuation and decision-making.

source.supporting_text: The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions. 3. Expected Learning Outcome of the Course: The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of financial analysis, advanced accounting practices, and valuation techniques. By the end of the program, learners will be able to effectively analyze financial statements, gaining insights into an organization's performance and financial health. A critical component of the curriculum focuses on valuation methods, where students will learn to assess the value of assets and investments using various approaches, such as discounted cash flow analysis and market comparables. This knowledge will empower them to evaluate investment opportunities critically and make informed decisions that can significantly impact an organization's financial strategy. Overall, these outcomes will prepare students for successful careers in finance and accounting, equipping them with both analytical and practical skills essential for navigating complex financial landscapes.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
scope: The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications.
description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

title: FINANCIAL ENGINEERING
scope: The objective of the course is to provide a preliminary understanding of financial engineering tools and techniques in the present market environment, such as applications of futures and options for hedging, asset price dynamics, and the use of simulation in decision-making. Financial Engineering is a multidisciplinary field involving financial theory, the methods of engineering, the tools of mathematics, and the practice of programming. The course on financial engineering would enable students to respond to the professional requirements particularly related to investment banking, financial management, treasury operations, asset management, risk management, consulting and capital markets, etc.
description: The Financial Engineering Concentration encompasses the design, analysis, and construction of financial contracts to meet the needs of enterprises. It involves developing and creatively applying financial theory and financial instruments to structure solutions to complex financial problems and exploit financial opportunities.

title: New Venture Creation
instructor: (Pilani & All Campuses)             : Prof. Jyoti Tikoria + Dr. Paul Lopez
scope: NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?
description: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.

title: RISK MANAGEMENT AND INSURANCE
scope: This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of this course is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing it. In this context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different classes of insurance. The objectives of the course are to provide students with  a comprehensive understanding for making risk management decisions to increase business value and individual welfare  a complete understanding of risk transfer through pooling and key features of insurance market  an understanding of the effects of and rationale for public policies that affect risk and its allocation  Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool.  Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization
description: Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention, risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation
makeup_policy: Make-up exams may be given only on genuine grounds and at the discretion of the instructor. Permission to take a make- up exam will depend upon the particular circumstances. Prior permission of I/C has to be obtained to get make-up.  Strictly, no makeup exams for quizzes/surprise class tests. Exam and quiz ground rules (additional ground rules may be announced at a later date).

scope.supporting_text: This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of this course is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing it. In this context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different classes of insurance. The objectives of the course are to provide students with  a comprehensive understanding for making risk management decisions to increase business value and individual welfare  a complete understanding of risk transfer through pooling and key features of insurance market  an understanding of the effects of and rationale for public policies that affect risk and its allocation  Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool.  Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization

description.supporting_text: Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention, risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation

title: Environmental Sampling and Analytical Methods
scope: The course introduces methodology of sample collection (sampling techniques) for water/wastewater/air. The course covers various aspects of sample analysis through conventional (for example gravimetric, titrimetric) and advanced methods (for example electrochemical, spectrophotometric, chromatographic). The course will also guide students, to apply concepts for environmental monitoring.
description: Principles of sample collection and data analysis/interpretation, Gravimetric methods, titrimetric methods, electrochemical methods, Spectrometric method of analysis, Chromatographic method of analysis, sampling techniques for air and water pollution, Biological methods of analysis, Interpretation of data in environmental monitoring.

title: Urban Water Management
scope: The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; (4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies.
description: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.

source.supporting_text: The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; (4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies.

description.supporting_text: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.

title: Electrical Machines
scope: Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer, DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts.
description: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
scope: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.
description: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).

scope.supporting_text: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.

description.supporting_text: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).

title: Microelectronic Circuits
scope: The objective of this course is to develop the ability to analyze and design integrated electronic circuits. The course aims to provide a thorough understanding of electronic circuits & building blocks necessary for the effective realization of analog integrated circuits. The course also includes the usage of SPICE as a circuit design aid.
description: Basic microelectronic circuit analysis and design, biasing in discrete and integrated circuit amplifiers, an overview of modeling of microelectronic devices single and two transistor amplifier configurations with passive and active loads; current mirrors & current sources; single-ended and differential linear amplifiers , differential and multistage amplifiers; 2 stage CMOS OPAMP, frequency response of amplifiers; negative feedback in amplifiers, R-C frequency compensation.

title: Communication Systems
scope: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.
description: Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization

source.supporting_text: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization

title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
scope: ⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic. ⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design. ⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential. ⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference Circuit. ⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs. ⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout. ⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments. ⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels of design abstraction. AUGSD/ AGSRD Division
description: This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area- efficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.

title: FPGA BASED SYSTEM DESIGN
scope: This course aims to upskill the students with the following topics:  Build a strong foundation in FPGA architecture, technologies, and design methodologies.  Develop proficiency in HDL-based design for creating complex digital systems.  Explore the full FPGA design flow—from concept to implementation and debugging.  Integrate embedded processors, IP cores, and DSP functions into FPGA-based designs.  Apply knowledge through hands-on labs and projects using modern FPGA platforms.
description: Digital system design options and trade-offs, design methodology and technology overview, Programmable Logic Devices, SPLDs, CPLDs, and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs); FPGA architectural options, granularity of function and wiring resources, coarse vs. fine-grained, vendor-specific issues (emphasis on Xilinx and Altera), Logic fabric, Look-up tables, block BRAMs, DSP slices etc., timing models, power dissipation, Input and Output cell characteristics, clock input, Timing, Power dissipation, Programmable interconnect, Hardware Description Languages, FPGA system design tools, synthesis, and implementation, design verification and debugging, FPGA based design studies, interfacing with input-output devices and data converters.

title: Data Communications and Networks
scope: A communication network is one of the fastest-growing areas today. The course introduces the concepts and mechanisms underlying the modern telecommunication systems and networks. The course is designed in such a way that the course is accessible to students without any special technical background in this area. The OSI model is used as a framework to introduce different protocols and standards. The course will prepare the student for advanced courses in the areas of telecommunication switching systems, computer networks, internetworking, etc.
description: Communication Concepts; Data and Voice Communications; Hardware Systems and Configurations; Network Topologies and Design Aspects; Protocols; Networking Local Area Networks; Network Security and Management; Emerging Trends in Communications.

title: Internet of Things
scope: This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wireless sensor networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors and actuators/ Communications and networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the course to solve real world problems. 3. Course learning Objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts, architectures, enabling technologies, communication protocols, data-management techniques, and security challenges associated with Internet of Things systems. b. Design and develop IoT-based solutions by integrating sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, communication networks, cloud platforms, and data-analytics tools. c. Apply practical programming and system-integration skills to build, test, and evaluate end-to-end IoT prototypes for addressing real-world applications such as smart cities, smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial automation.
description: Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points, Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies. This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE), B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL).

title: Modern Control Systems
description: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains. 2. Scopes and Objectives After completing this course the students will be able to 1) Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems 2) Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain 3) Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains 4) Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool) 5) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm 6) Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones 3. Prescribed Text/ Reference Books 1. Control Systems by I.K. Nagrath and M. Gopal, New Age 2. Control Systems Engineering by Norman Nise, John Wiley 3. Modern Control Theory by M. Gopal, New Age 4. Systems and Control by S.H. Zak, OUP 5. Modern Control Design with Matlab and Simulink by Ashish Tewari, John Wiley Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary

title: Fiber Optics and Optoelectronics
scope: In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers, sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for communication applications.
description: Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and applications); modulators (electro- optic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul communications; fiber optic networks.

scope.supporting_text: In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers, sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for communication applications.

description.supporting_text: Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and applications); modulators (electro- optic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul communications; fiber optic networks.

title: Digital Image Processing
scope: Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday technology.
description: This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition.

title: Semiconductor Fabrication Technology
scope: This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges across various disciplines.
description: The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be discussed in detail.

title: Satellite Communications
scope: This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or- bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link- budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed- assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.
description: Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO, MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications.

scope.supporting_text: This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or- bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link- budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed- assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.

description.supporting_text: Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO, MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications.

title: RF AND MICROWAVE CIRCUIT DESIGN
scope: Identify basic RF devices/components and their applications, understand common rules of thumb in RF design, use scattering matrix for RF network analysis, design planar transmission lines, design impedance-matching circuits, use the Smith chart for impedance matching, implement passive RF devices in planar technology, design passive RF devices with RF CAD tools, learn the use of a vector network analyzer for RF measurements, learn the basic principles of RF amplifier
description: Introduction to radio frequency engineering; advantages; various frequency bands; applications; Microwave passive components and high frequency modeling; Microwave network analysis: scattering parameters and Signal flow graph; vector network analyzer-dynamic range and IF bandwidth; Transmission lines; microstrip lines; impedance matching techniques-transmission line based and lumped circuit approach and layout generation. Power dividers and couplers, RF filter design; Filter scaling and transformation; Filter implementation using microstrip lines and lumped components; Amplifier design; noise, harmonic distortion, and intercept point analysis, amplifier design for gain and noise figure; oscillator design, one-port and two- port oscillator design, phase noise of oscillator, introduction to EMI and EMC, recent trends.

Instructions  The Quiz (short test) will be conducted during the lecture hour, which will be announced a week earlier  Students will perform the Lab simulations individually.  Simulation problems for practice will be uploaded in Nalanda. Students will maintain a lab record of the simulations, with the write-up of Objectives, Principles, Design, CAD model, Results and Conclusion. The record will be evaluated thoroughly for its originality, correctness, technical integrity, and neatness.  Students’ RF design skills will be tested by assigning design problems, which will be rigorously evaluated.

title: Embedded System Design
scope: The course intends to introduce the various components of an embedded system and embedded system design considerations. title: Real-Time Embedded Systems
scope: Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and design issues of Real-time systems. The course focuses on the basics of Hardware design, advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Specifically we discuss the Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc.
description: This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software design, Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems.
