title: Signal Theory and Optimization
scope: The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties, limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables. The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen _ Instruction Division value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers, numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques. The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random signals and related theory, ii) linear algebra, matrices iii) optimization techniques and their uses in communications and signal processing.
description: Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes; stationarity, autocorrelation, ergodicity, and power spectral density; basic concepts of linear algebra: vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition; matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and numerical optimization techniques.

title: Modelling and Analysis of Electrical Machines
scope: The objective of the course is to comprehend and analyse the steady-state, transient and dynamic behaviour of electrical machines using mathematical models, and also to familiarize the students about advanced modelling. The course will develop students’ understanding on modelling of electrical machines from conventional methods to advanced methods through generalized theory of electrical machines. Furthermore, the students will appreciate the scope and applicability of course with the help of hands-on practice using simulation tools and hardware setup, encouraging and strengthening their ability to approach and investigate important challenges of automation and e-mobility associated to research interests of industries and academia, for example, digital-twin, model predictive modelling and control, fault analysis, predictive maintenance, and advanced control. The prerequisite of this course is, to have a basic understanding of electrical circuits, electrical machines and control systems; mainly modelling of physical systems.
description: Review of Rotating Electrical Machines, Element of Generalized Theory of Rotating Electrical Machines, Linear transformation and Reference-frame Theory, DC Machines, Three-phase Synchronous Machines, Three-phase Induction Machines, Special Machines, Introduction to motor parameters estimation and model generation using MATLAB

title: Fundamentals of Optoelectronics
instructor: Prof. Rahul Kumar (IC), Prof. Navneet Gupta, Prof. V. K. Chaubey
description: This course introduces the principles, design, and applications of optoelectronic devices. The course begins with a description of the interaction of light with semiconductor materials in a p-n junction configuration. This includes the phenomena of absorption, electroluminescence, and stimulated emission. The distinction between direct and indirect semiconductor materials is noted. Basic devices are then described: photodiodes, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), semiconductor optical amplifiers, and laser diodes. Array detectors, including complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) and charge-coupled devices (CCD) arrays, and array LEDs are then introduced. Basic specifications and applications of each of these devices are described, including solar cells, imaging with array detectors, and LED displays.

title: EEE G554
scope: a. Understand the concept of resonant tank network b. Analyze the dependence of ZVS/ZCS boundary on load resistance c. Design ZVS/ZCS switch cell for DC-DC converter d. Analysis of switching loss and EMI under soft switching
description: This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero-current- switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course.

title: Power Quality
scope: A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems.
description: This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.

scope.supporting_text: A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems.

description.supporting_text: This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.

title: NANO-ELECTRONICS AND NANO-PHOTONICS TECHNOLOGY
scope: This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.
description: Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology.

title: Advanced Wireless Communications
scope: a) This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next- generation wireless networks. b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks. c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless communications. d) New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next-generation wireless networks, like D2D communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.
description: Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in wireless communications.

scope.supporting_text: a) This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next- generation wireless networks. b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks. c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless communications. d) New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next-generation wireless networks, like D2D communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.

title: Advanced Digital Communication
description: Introduction to digital communication systems; signal characterization and representation of bandpass and low-pass signals; signal space analysis; fundamentals of source coding and entropy; digital modulation techniques and constellation design; optimum receivers for additive white Gaussian noise channels; maximum likelihood (ML) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection; symbol error probability analysis; non-coherent detection methods; carrier and symbol synchronization techniques; communication over band-limited channels; ISI, Nyquist criteria, and signal waveform design, equalization; multicarrier modulation systems, effects of intercarrier interference (ICI) and carrier frequency offset (CFO); channel capacity limits and fundamentals of channel coding. 2. Course Scope and Objective: 1. To provide fundamental knowledge to model, design, and analyze advanced digital communication systems, with applications in both industry and R&D. 2. To reinforce theoretical concepts through practical assignments using MATLAB, Python, and USRP. 3. Requires prior knowledge of Linear Systems, Probability Theory, Stochastic Processes, and basic Communication Systems.

title: Hardware and Software Codesign
scope: This course deals with the system-level design of embedded systems comprised of both hardware and software. It investigates topics ranging from system modeling to hardware-software implementation. This course also teaches analysis and optimization processes for supporting algorithmic and architectural design decisions. It also helps the student gain design experience through different case studies. The course emphasizes a top-down design methodology driven by bottom-up constraints. The topics covered will include co-design of hardware and software involving key aspects like partitioning, mapping and optimization. 2. Course Learning Objectives (CLOs) are as follows a. Analyze embedded system requirements and develop suitable hardware–software co-design solutions by applying system-level modeling, partitioning, and synthesis techniques. b. Evaluate and optimize hardware–software architectures using partitioning algorithms, mapping strategies, and performance estimation methods to satisfy design constraints such as speed, area, power, and cost. c. Design and implement hardware–software co-designed embedded applications using contemporary design methodologies and FPGA-based platforms to address real-world engineering problems.

title: Modern Control Systems
description: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains. 2. Scopes and Objectives After completing this course the students will be able to 1) Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems 2) Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain 3) Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains 4) Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool) 5) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm 6) Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones 3. Prescribed Text/ Reference Books 1. Control Systems by I.K. Nagrath and M. Gopal, New Age 2. Control Systems Engineering by Norman Nise, John Wiley 3. Modern Control Theory by M. Gopal, New Age 4. Systems and Control by S.H. Zak, OUP 5. Modern Control Design with Matlab and Simulink by Ashish Tewari, John Wiley Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary

title: Hydraulic and Fluid Mechanics
scope: This course introduces the foundational principles of fluid mechanics and their practical applications in hydraulic systems used in water and wastewater treatment plants and sewerage networks. It covers the behavior of fluids in motion and at rest, emphasizing both theoretical frameworks and engineering applications. Topics include flow regimes, pressure losses, open channel flow, pump performance, and hydraulic modeling. Students will develop analytical skills to solve real-world fluid flow problems and design efficient hydraulic systems.
description: Dimensions, units, dimensionless ratios, hydraulic similarity and the testing of models, Continuity and Bernoulli's equations, fluid properties, Reynolds experiment, laminar and turbulent flow in pipes, major and minor losses in flow through pipes, Flow in pipelines between reservoirs, open channel flow, Pumps, flow and velocity measurement devices.

title: Environmental Chemistry and Environmental Biotechnology
instructor: and other instructor   : Prof. Bibhas R. Sarkar (IC), and Prof. B. Vani
description: The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern industrialized ecology. Learning Objectives The course will be broadly divided based on the three major components as hydrosphere, atmosphere and geosphere. Learning objectives for each of the broad topics as discussed in the course plan has been described along with – what the learner should be able to do by studying these.

title: [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]
scope: The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.
description: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.

title: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management
scope: The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications.
description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. title: Financial Management
scope: This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel.
description: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.

title: Financial Risk Analytics and Management
scope: The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document.
description: This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk management roles. Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory, Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk with Derivatives.

title: Modern Political Concepts
scope: This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political thought. This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical skills, and the understanding of human diversity. Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political discourses. However, the students are encouraged to move beyond the textbook and familiarize with the research studies by eminent scholars. This course encourages to use critical thinking and evidence to understand and evaluate rival theories and interpretations. Accordingly, Students are expected to participate in the classroom discussions as well as initiate and moderate discussions on political issues that may have captivated their interest. This practice enables students to develop a critical understanding of various political discourses and equip them to address political theories and questions of political life and values. Most significantly, this Course facilitates students’ engagement with various political debates of contemporary India and the world.

title: Environment, Development and Climate Change (EDCC)
scope: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the debates and issues relating to sustainable development and climate change, so as to sufficiently challenge them to come up with practical solutions. The course covers theory and practice at the global and local levels and examines the contemporary policy and practice regarding environment, development and climate change.
description: This course focuses on the concepts of environment, development, and climate change in the contemporary world. The nature and causes of environmental problems in developing and developed countries will be explored. Attention is given to both the causes and solutions of environmental problems and the role of state and non-state actors interacting at local, national and global scales. The goal of this course is for the learners to appreciate the people-environment relations and to understand the anthropocentric dynamics of development and climate change.

title: Development Theories
scope: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the debates and issues relating to development and post development. The course covers development theory and practice at the global and local levels and examines the practice in contemporary times. . Text Books: John Rapley (2010), Understanding Development: Theory and Practice in the Third World Viva Books. (Reading material will be given by the IC through classroom portal)
description: This course focuses on the concept of development, development theories and practices in the modern world. Interplay between theory and practice and the outcome of this relationship are also explored in the syllabus. The course provides an overview of development thinking from ‘classical’ development ideas to alternative and post development theories. The course then attempts to critically review contemporary debates about development, including the link between the current world order and the Development goals of the developing countries.

title: PRINT & AUDIO-VISUAL ADVERTISING
scope: a. To introduce advertising with IMC perspectives b. To engage the students through various hands-on activities relating to Advertising Media c. To prepare the students to learn advertising concepts and theories in practice d. To expose the students to the traditional and digital media for advertising e. To familiarize the students about global advertising and promotion scenario along with rural marketing f. To sensitize them about various ethical issues when planning and implementing advertising and promotional programs g. To underscore the implications of AI within advertising realm
description: The course is planned to give a comprehensive working knowledge of Advertising and Marketing communication and how they inter-relate. It offers modules, case studies and do-it your own assignment opportunities. The main feature of the course is that it is constantly evolving, keeping itself relevant to the needs of the advertising industry. Today’s student is expected to understand all the major marketing functions: advertising, its process, integrated marketing communication involving across multimedia: podcast/podcasts, newspaper, magazine, television, and via Internet. It aims to enable the students to familiarize the advertising communication process and how it works in relation to market and the consumers.

title: Creative Writing
scope: The objective of the course is to familiarize students with the nature and functioning of creative writing. Besides basic tenets of creative writing, the course will not only encourage the students to acquire techniques of constructing events, characters, writing poems, short stories and one act plays but also develop in them the ability to appreciate writings of all sorts. References to the related and contemporary works will be made from time to time during discussion and workshop.
description: Principles of creative writing, stimulating creative activity, techniques of creating images, constructing events and creating characters, writing short stories, digital storytelling and multimodal narratives, plays and poems, adaptation of creative writing across digital and social media, writing critical essays on works of art, AI and digital writing tools, authorship and ethics

title: Current Affairs
scope: The objectives of the course are to instill in students the habit of keeping themselves updated on a host of issues that relate not only to an individual but the society at large and also to inculcate among the students the skills of reading, understanding, interpreting and forming an opinion on national and international events and issues of different nature and of various domains. 3. LearningOutcomes: Having successfully completed all the modules of the course, students will be able to a. Read about, listen to, interpret and understand current issues covered in print, visual and electronic media b. Analyze an issue from various perspectives and understand their implications for an individual, a nation and the society at large c. Identify ideological biases in people’s opinion d. Form informed opinion on any given issue e. Express opinion in an effective manner
description: Introduction to, Importance and scope of Current Affairs; Domains of Current Affairs-Political, Social, Religious, Scientific, Developmental, etc.;Issues in Current Affairs-Controversial, Non-controversial, Neutral; Sources of Information in Current Affairs-newspapers, Magazines, Posters, Pamphlets, Manifestoes, recently published books, etc.; Reading: Skimming & Scanning, Extensive vs. Intensive, comprehension;Understanding current issues, events and information; Interpreting current issues, events and information; Opinion formation-factors and materials influencing opinion formation;Balancing and expressing opinion.

scope.supporting_text: The objectives of the course are to instill in students the habit of keeping themselves updated on a host of issues that relate not only to an individual but the society at large and also to inculcate among the students the skills of reading, understanding, interpreting and forming an opinion on national and international events and issues of different nature and of various domains. 3. LearningOutcomes: Having successfully completed all the modules of the course, students will be able to a. Read about, listen to, interpret and understand current issues covered in print, visual and electronic media b. Analyze an issue from various perspectives and understand their implications for an individual, a nation and the society at large c. Identify ideological biases in people’s opinion d. Form informed opinion on any given issue e. Express opinion in an effective manner

description.supporting_text: Introduction to, Importance and scope of Current Affairs; Domains of Current Affairs-Political, Social, Religious, Scientific, Developmental, etc.;Issues in Current Affairs-Controversial, Non-controversial, Neutral; Sources of Information in Current Affairs-newspapers, Magazines, Posters, Pamphlets, Manifestoes, recently published books, etc.; Reading: Skimming & Scanning, Extensive vs. Intensive, comprehension;Understanding current issues, events and information; Interpreting current issues, events and information; Opinion formation-factors and materials influencing opinion formation;Balancing and expressing opinion.

title: Effective Public Speaking
scope: The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy, audience suitability, bias, and ethical use. 3. Classroom Methodology The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal, and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice-oriented and develops speaking skills through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and presentation tasks. Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.
description: Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non- Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering- Effective Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion and Job Interviews

title: Introduction to Conflict Management
scope: To develop the knowledge and professional skills necessary to facilitate resolution of conflicts. Emphasis would be laid on skills and specific techniques to resolve inter-personal, organizational and community-based conflicts. At the conclusion of the course, the student will understand the basic dynamics of conflict, most significant interventions used to manage conflict, benefits and costs of conflict, recognize his or her preferred style of conflict management and develop an understanding and appreciation of the conflict management styles of others.
description: Nature and dynamics of conflict; characteristics of conflict; theories of conflict; reasons and sources of conflict; value of conflict in social change; different approaches to addressing and managing conflict; conflict analysis through socio-economic class; class-based dimensions of conflict; culture and globalization perspectives; role of culture in propagating conflict; role of globalization in nation-state conflict; workplace and organizational conflict dynamics; conformity theories and conflict; power of communication; identity-based perspectives on conflict; AI, technology, and conflict resolution; algorithmic and digital dimensions of conflict; negotiation techniques; mitigation and resolution techniques; conflict management styles.

title: Marxian Thought
scope: Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without fundamentally exploitative structures. 3. Primary Text and Viewing Material: Selections from these books and viewing material will be used based on the requirements of the class. o A Reader’s Guide to Marx’s Capital - Joseph Choonara o Chapters from Yanis Varoufakis o Selected Readings from Ha-Joon Chang Film Clippings for Class Discussion: Mandi, Yashowardhan Mishra (2019); Rang de Basanti (2006); Bread and Roses, Ken Loach (2000); The Wind that Shakes the Barley, Ken Loach (2006); Nae Pasaran, Felipe Bustos Sierra (2018)
description: This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures.

title: Critical Analysis of Literature and Cinema
scope: The course attempts to inculcate in students a critical insight required to interpret a work of literature or cinema. To enable the students to imbibe such perception and critical judgment, the subtle nuances of such works will be taught extensively. Students will also be introduced to different forms, terminologies and trends prevalent in such artistic ventures to enable them to place a work of art in the proper context.
description: Creativity and Aesthetics; Overview of Approaches to Literature, Interpretation of Selected Works; Cinema; Understanding Drama: Theme, Character, Plot, Form; Understanding Fiction: Setting, Point of View, Plot and Character; Understanding Short Fiction and Novel: Meaning and Message, Style and Coherence; Understanding Comics; Understanding Cinema: Relationship of Form and Meaning, Image Construction, Shots, Scenes, Sequences, Mise-en-Scene, Codes, Frames, Signs, Syntax; Sound: Diegetic & Non-diegetic Sound, Silence; Linear and Non-linear Narrative Structure.

title: TECHNIQUES IN SOCIAL RESEARCH
scope: This course seeks to provide knowledge and skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data.
description: Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance, dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement, reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation, inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics).

scope.supporting_text: The objective of the course is to acquaint students with the practical and theoretical issues associated with computer- mediated communication (CMC) systems. The focus of the course will be on CMC and its influence on society as a mode of communication.

description.supporting_text: Computer Mediated Communication- Definitions and overview; Evolution of Computer Mediated Communication; Components of Computer Mediated Communication; Computer Mediated Discourse Analysis- Theories and faceted Approach; Information-Interactivity Dynamism in Computer Mediated Communication; Gender perspectives in Computer Mediated Communication; Privacy Issues in Computer Mediated Communication; Socialization in Social Media-Profiles, Identity and traversal; Computer Mediated Communication and technology acceptance; Computer Mediated Communication Theories; Human-Computer Interfaces.

title: COPYWRITING
scope: • To introduce the concept of copywriting in advertising • To connect the various advertising concepts and theories to the art of copywriting • To generate ideas for successful business copy • To prepare the students to learn business content writing • To uncover the basics of the traditional and digital media for copywriting • to expose the students through various hands on copy activities relating to different media • To learn to write ethically and value driven copy for sustainable business 3. Prescribed Text book: June A. Valladares. The Craft of Copywriting. Response Books, New Delhi, 2007.
description: Copywriting is the corner stone of ALL successful marketing. Copywriting empowers you with the ability to turn words into dollars. Effective copy can play an important role in shaping perceptions about products, services and brands. The course requires a sound knowledge of advertising communications and will explore all aspects of writing for print, radio, television and online. It extensively prepares the students to write and develop ad copy for various media while selecting tone(s), style(s) and approach(es) for ad copy.…It further equips the students to communicate the strategy and specific assignments to a team using a Creative Brief.

title: Readings from Drama
scope: The objective of the course is to introduce students to different types and forms of drama. In doing so, this course will familiarize students with various dramatic forms spanning different geographical spaces and time, thereby helping them to have a deeper understanding of the same. It will also enable the students to connect various dramatic forms through the study of visuals, timelines, and biographical and contextual readings that allow them to delve further into the history and conventions of the time period when these dramatic works were produced.
description: Drama as a distinct genre; History of drama; Performance and stagecraft; Evolution of drama from a theocentric to a logocentric plane; Distinct characteristics of Western and non-Western dramas; Aristotle’s Poetics and the genre of tragedy; Bharat Muni’s Natyashastra and the idea of comedy; Adaptation of myths as Drama; Modern drama.

scope: The objective of the course is to acquaint students with the nature and functioning of language and the role it plays in the society. The fundamental linguistic concepts will be exemplified through English. Reference to Indian languages will also be made whenever possible.

title: Introductory Philosophy
scope: A critical survey of major Western and Indian philosophical viewpoints, from antiquity to contemporary thought. The course aims to equip students with the tools to critically evaluate philosophical arguments and to appreciate their relevance to questions of knowledge, ethics, and selfhood in human life. 3. Course Learning Objectives Upon completion of the course students will have • An understanding of the various philosophical schools of Indian and Western traditions. • A critical and comparative grasp of the philosophical viewpoints & debates. • An ability to build theoretical constructions and extend philosophical thinking to other disciplines. • An ability to practice the habit of thinking rationally and critically in leading an ethical and meaningful life
description: An overview of major philosophical traditions from the Western and Indian worlds. The course traces the nature and purpose of philosophy from classical Greek thought through modern rationalism, empiricism, and existentialism before turning to the classical Indian schools.

title: Popular Literature and Culture of South Asia
scope: The objective of the course is to introduce students to Literature and Popular Culture of South Asia. In doing so, it will familiarize students to perspectives and scenarios that differ from their own culture, thereby, helping them to have deeper understanding of other cultures. This course aims to bridge the gaps in our understanding of our neighbors and enable us to have broader perspectives.
description: South Asia as a region; culture and its representation through literature and cinema; politics of representation, breaking the stereotypes; bringing in the marginalized voices; writings of women; identity formation; concept of majority and minority; commonality in spite of all the differences, violence, migration and dislocation.

scope: To develop a conceptual framework for understanding organizations and their various functions from a psychological viewpoint. title: SCIENCE FICTION
scope: i) Introduce students to science fiction as a literary mode that critiques technological and social change. ii) Explore how science fiction engages with questions of environment and the posthuman through narrative. iii) Examine connections between science, technology, and ethics through speculative imagination. iv) Develop interdisciplinary skills by linking literary analysis with perspectives from history of science and cultural studies.
description: Key concepts and histories of science fiction; major theoretical frameworks in SF; utopias, dystopias, and speculative futures; science fiction in relation to technological and ecological change; feminist, postcolonial, and global interventions in SF; engagements with artificial intelligence, posthumanism, and the animal; and the reimagining of cultural and ecological futures through speculative storytelling.
makeup_policy: Will be allowed if there is a genuine reason and the student reaches out to me promptly.

title: Human Resource Development
description: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of the practical ramification (or better subfield) of human resource management and deals with the significant issues related to developing human resources with special reference to its tripartite foundations of human betterment, organizational enhancement, and societal development. The course will help clarify the subtle difference between HR Management & HR Development. This will also enable curious minds to learn more about how training programs are planned, conceived, constructed, and delivered to potential stakeholders. HRD focuses on this core idea as to how the capabilities and credentials (and ultimately productivity) of the employees can be enhanced.
makeup_policy: No Make-up Requests would be entertained with only exception being medical.

title: Musicology - An - Introduction
scope: The course aims to acquaint the students with the how and why of Music. It introduces the concepts of Musicology, Applied Theory, Rasa-Bhava and the working of Raga, Acoustics, some aspects of the textual and contextual development of music, the semantics of music, influence of music over mind and body, composers and compositions.
description: Preliminary Lecture, Logic and Science working behind music, Interval of Frequencies and interval of time, Scales- Hindustani, Carnatic and Western, Musical Streams, Notation Systemes, Principles of Thaat, Raga and Taal, Multiple speeds (Layakari), Philosophy and Psychology of music, Aesthetics of music, Voice Culture.

title: SRIMAD BHAGAVAD GITA
scope: Meant for anyone who wants to make his or her life peaceful, blissful and perfect by aligning oneself to the principles set forth in Srimad Bhagavad Gita. The prime objectives of this course are to understand our relationship (sambhandha) with God, the process of reviving that relationship (abhidheya), and the goal of that process (prayojana). In this context, the 5 important subject matter isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma are discussed in detail. 3. Course Learning Objectives Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: 1. Explain the principal philosophical concepts of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, including isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala, and karma, and the relationship among them. 2. Differentiate and analyse the major paths of yoga—karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, dhyana-yoga, and bhakti-yoga—along with their purpose and practical significance. 3. Apply the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita to improve time management, stress management, concentration, emotional balance, self-discipline, decision-making, and overall well-being in academic and personal life. _
description: This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices, viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth), dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti- yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge.

title: Professional Ethics
scope: This course provides a formal acquaintance with the concepts and frameworks of ethics; recognize the codes of ethics relevant to the experience of being a professional and develops an understanding of the ethical issues relating to professions generally, and to business, management, education, engineering, and computing in particular. Through the analysis of real-time case studies, students learn to appreciate the role of moral reasoning in issues of professional life. 3. Course Learning Objectives: Upon completion of the course students will have ● An understanding of the core concepts of ethics, the profession, and professional ethics, and their specific application across business, management, education, engineering, and computing. ● A critical and comparative grasp of competing ethical theories and professional viewpoints such as rule- following versus professional judgment. ● An ability to apply ethical theories and frameworks to real, contested professional dilemmas, extending this reasoning across multiple professional domains rather than any single one. ● An ability to practice the habit of sound ethical judgment and professional responsibility in one's own future career and conduct.
description: An introduction to the ethical concepts, theories, and codes that govern professional life. The course traces the foundations of ethics and the profession, before applying this framework across business, management, education, engineering, and computing.

title: INTERNATIONALRELATIONS
scope: International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.
description:  Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, China’s entry into WTO.  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and Global Governance  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.  Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR  India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and United States.

description.supporting_text:  Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, China’s entry into WTO.  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and Global Governance  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.  Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR  India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and United States.

title: ECOCRITICISM
scope: 1. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends. 2. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts. 3. To equip the students to create ecocritical documents in literary, cinematic and other artistic forms. 4. To train the learners in the application of the critical concepts to various cultural texts.
description: Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well- being of our planet.

title: Academic Writing Lab
description: AI-supported, process-oriented, portfolio-intensive academic writing practice; AI-assisted drafting support, editing and feedback evaluation with emphasis on originality and academic integrity; writing process stages including planning, drafting, feedback, revision and reflection; structured writing portfolio with drafts, feedback and revision evidence; idea generation with a focus on clarity of thought; paragraph construction with topic sentences; logical sequencing and paragraph linking; organizational patterns including cause–effect, comparison, problem–solution and process description; text interpretation and transformation through summarizing, paraphrasing and originality maintenance; academic vocabulary; genre-based writing: analytical paragraphs, short essays, reflective responses, structured reports, data commentaries and case studies; visual information integration into writing; revision strategies for accuracy improvement; disciplinary and real-world contextualization of writing; reflective writing practices. Scope: Hands-on-practice for specific academic written genres, formative feedback using AI tools, and continuous assessment. Course Objective: This course focuses on enabling the students to: 1. Produce coherent and well-structured texts across academic and professional genres; 2. Apply organizational patterns and paragraph development strategies for clear and logical writing; 3. Demonstrate accuracy in sentence structure, grammar, punctuation, and academic vocabulary; 4. Utilize AI tools effectively to edit writing; 5. Revise writing keeping in view task requirements.

title: Electrical Machines
scope: Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer, DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better understanding of the concepts.
description: Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.

title: ELECTRONIC DEVICES
scope: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.
description: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).

scope.supporting_text: The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.

description.supporting_text: (as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).

course_codes.supporting_text: Course No. : EEE F266/ INSTR F266/ECE F266

title: Electronic Instruments and Instrumentation Technology
scope:  An introduction to measurement techniques and instrumentation design and operation  The basic concept of units, measurement error and accuracy, the construction and design of measuring devices and circuits, measuring instruments and their proper applications  To learn about instrument design aspects, techniques and specifications of various electronic instruments  To know various aspects of Industrial Communication techniques
description: An introduction to measurement techniques and instrumentation design and operation, the basic concept of units, measurement error and accuracy, Instrument design aspects, techniques and specifications of electronic instruments, the construction and design of measuring devices and measuring instruments such as Analog/ Digital meters, DSO, signal generators, signal analyzers, data loggers and recorders, electronic counters with their proper applications, Industrial Communication techniques, safety methods and instrumentation in hazardous areas. The course will also consist of laboratory practice and lab assignments.

title: Transducers and Measurement Systems
scope: The objective of this course is to have a detailed study of measurement systems and to understand their application in the areas of monitoring, control and experimental engineering analysis.
description: INSTR F312 Transducers and Measurement Systems Importance and types of measurement, generalized measurement system, functional elements, static and dynamic characteristics, primary sensing elements, modulating transducers, self generating transducers, inverse transducers, fiber optic transducers, measurement techniques for motion, seismic, pressure, flow, temperature, level, humidity, pH, viscosity; charge, isolation amplifier, MEMS based transducers;

scope.supporting_text: The objective of this course is to have a detailed study of measurement systems and to understand their application in the areas of monitoring, control and experimental engineering analysis.

description.supporting_text: INSTR F312 Transducers and Measurement Systems Importance and types of measurement, generalized measurement system, functional elements, static and dynamic characteristics, primary sensing elements, modulating transducers, self generating transducers, inverse transducers, fiber optic transducers, measurement techniques for motion, seismic, pressure, flow, temperature, level, humidity, pH, viscosity; charge, isolation amplifier, MEMS based transducers;

title.supporting_text: Course Title : Transducers and Measurement Systems

title: ANALOG AND DIGITAL VLSI DESIGN
scope: ⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic. ⮚ Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design. ⮚ Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential. ⮚ Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference Circuit. ⮚ Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs. ⮚ Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout. ⮚ Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments. ⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels of design abstraction. AUGSD/ AGSRD Division
description: This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area- efficient, and high-performance circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.

title: Linear Algebra and its Applications
scope: Linear algebra has applications in pure and applied mathematics, computer science, economics, engineering, mathematical biology, operation research, physics, and statistics. Linear algebra and matrix methods are also important for data analysis. Linear Algebra and its applications typically aim to equip students with a solid understanding of fundamental concepts in linear algebra and the ability to apply these concepts to the above fields.
description: uick review of Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations, Basis and Dimension, Q rank-nullity theorem, change of basis; Inner product spaces, Cauchy Schwarz's inequality, GramSchmidt orthonormalization, QR decomposition, Discrete Fourier Transform, and their applications, Spectral Theorem, Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, Decomposition theorem, and Jordan canonical forms, applications of SVD in Principal Component Analysis, use of SVD in low-rank approximations and to find least-squares solutions.

scope: a) Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object- oriented analysis and design, and design patterns. b) In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on tools like Eclipse. c) The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.
description: Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object model: classes, objects, methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification, analysis and design; notations for object-oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some object oriented programming languages. Object Oriented Design Patterns: Behavioural, Structural and Creational.

title: Discrete Mathematics
scope: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms.
description: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs.

title: ALGEBRA I
scope: The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together. We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from number theory, linear algebra and geometry.
description: Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and polynomials over the rational field.

title: Foundations of Data Science
description: This course introduces the mathematical foundations of data science with emphasis on probability, Gaussian models, statistical inference, nonparametric methods, optimization, dimensionality reduction, data preparation, and scalable data analytics. It develops core tools such as probability bounds, Bayesian inference, PCA and SVD, kernel density estimation, nearest-neighbor methods, and connects them to practical data-analysis problems.

title: Mathematical Modelling
scope: The principal objective of this course is to familiarize students with the theory of population and a basic understanding of mathematical modelling of a real-world problem. Students will gain enough background to read theoretical population and evolutionary ecology literature, do simple modelling, and springboard to more complex theory if desired. Students will develop techniques for understanding and analysing simple, multivariate, and nonlinear models will be explored.
description: Mathematical Modeling in Biology, Epidemiology, Model for Various Problems and Situation Using ODE and PDE, Classic Models in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Equilibria and Stability Analysis, Dynamics of Class-Structured Populations, Techniques for Analyzing Models.

title: Multivariable Calculus
scope:  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.
description: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
