title: OPTIMIZATION
scope: Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of making trade-offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems have become well-established and are encountered in the physical sciences, engineering, economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems. This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms.
description: Introduction to optimization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality and sensitivity analysis; transportation model and its variants; integer linear programming nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques.

title: Discrete Mathematics
scope: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms.
description: Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets, lattices and Boolean algebras; Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques; Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations, generating function, partitions; Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and Hamilton graphs.

title: ALGEBRA I
scope: The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together. We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from number theory, linear algebra and geometry.
description: Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and polynomials over the rational field.

title: Ordinary Differential Equations
instructor: BALRAM DUBEY, Email: bdubey@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, Chamber No: 6067-B
scope: Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science, engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues to address and various approaches to choose from: Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions? Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances. Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of solutions and do not require solving the differential equation. Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life.
description: Existence and uniqueness theorems; properties of linear systems; behavior of solutions of nth order equations; asymptotic behavior of linear systems; stability of linear and weakly nonlinear systems; conditions for boundedness and the number of zeros of the nontrivial solutions of second order equations; stability by Lyapunov's direct method; autonomous and non-autonomous systems.

title: Combinatorial Mathematics
scope: Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete. What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting.
description: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems: “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach.

The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting.

description.supporting_text: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems: “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach.

title: Applied Statistical Methods
scope: This 4th level course is designed with a two-fold purpose. First, it will provide an exposure to various theoretical univariate/multivariate methods and their practical applications. Second, this course will improve methodological/analytical maturity to attempt a variety of problems using MS-excel and R.
description: Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statis- tical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, re- alizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinter- pretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference, analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R.

title: Multivariable Calculus
scope:  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.
description: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.

title: Fluid Mechanics
scope: The objectives of the course are to learn about the following topics: • Introduction to fluid mechanics and establish its relevance in mechanical engineering. • Derivation of the equations governing mass, momentum and energy transport. • Application of the governing equation to solve simple fluid mechanics problems. • Non-dimensionalization of governing equations and identification of dimensionless numbers, Modeling and similarity concepts. • Two dimensional, inviscid, potential flows; Stream function, Velocity potential. • Analyze laminar and turbulent flows inside pipes, External flow past immersed bodies, Intro- duction to Boundary layer theory • One dimensional, compressible flow inside ducts of variable cross-section, normal and oblique shocks.
description: This course covers the following topics: Mathematical preliminaries; Fluid statics and forces on submerged bodies; Integral relations for a control volume; Mass, Momentum and Energy Con- servation; Reynolds Transport Theorem; Differential relations for fluid flow, Analytical solution of Navier-Stokes equation; Dimensional analysis and similarity; Inviscid potential flows; Bernoulli’s Equation; Internal and external viscous flows; Basic compressible flows.

title: DESIGN OF MACHINE ELEMENTS
scope: To prepare a student of mechanical engineering to apply theory and practice of Design of Mechanical Elements. It is an introductory course laying foundation on design ground rules, application of strength of material principles, selection of components, and selection of materials for a given application.
description: The course introduces students to concepts and nuances of Mechanical Engineering Design. Content includes materials, standards and design of machine elements and application of scientific principles, technical knowledge, and imaginative skills to be developed in a student. The machine elements covered are Shafts, Screw fasteners, Welded joints, Springs, Brakes & Clutches, Bearings and Gears. The Tutorial classes of the course will be mainly used for assisted problem solving, consultation and evaluation.

title: [Advanced Manufacturing Processes]
scope: This course introduces students to advanced manufacturing technologies for fabricating components across multiple length scales. It focuses on the challenges of machining difficult- to-machine materials and transforming them into high-value products. The course emphasizes hands-on learning through CNC part programming, CNC machine operation, additive manufacturing, and digital-to-physical manufacturing workflows. Lectures complement laboratory sessions by covering the fundamentals, process capabilities, numerical methods, and optimization techniques required for the analysis and development of advanced manufacturing processes.
description: Unconventional manufacturing processes and analysis, micro-manufacturing technologies, introduction to computer-aided manufacturing, CNC machines, CNC Part programming, additive manufacturing, modelling and simulation of manufacturing processes, surface technologies, related laboratory exercise and fabrication project.

title: Engines, Motors, and Mobility
scope: This course has been designed to make the students familiar with internal combustion engines and electric and hybrid electric power trains.
description: The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck, locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric vehicles.

title: Data Mining in Mechanical Sciences
scope: The primary focus of this course is on application of data mining methods in mechanical sciences and engineering. Following are the details objectives of this course: • Understanding the fundamental of data mining. • Building mathematical foundation for data mining. • Knowledge of data capturing to minimize the information losses. • Understanding of patterns in data, data classification and clustering. • Knowledge of application of identified patterns in data in fields like in-processing monitoring, machine monitoring, defect analysis, machine and maintenance scheduling etc. • Understanding of different prediction methods based on the data processing. • Understand the difference between artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning. • Knowledge of which data mining methods should be used for what type of data. • Understanding the concept of big data in mechanical and manufacturing domain and how to handle it.
description: Introduction to data mining, clustering, classification & association, sequence analysis, regressions method, decision trees, machine learning, neural networks, SVM for engineering and manufacturing applications, data mining for product design, applications of data mining in production, planning and scheduling, data mining for defect identification, process and quality control, application of data mining in maintenance, data analysis for machine and manufacturing process monitoring, introduction to cyber physical systems, introduction to big data handling and big data analytics.

title: Energy Storage Technologies
scope: The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior.
description: This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.

scope.supporting_text: The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior.

description.supporting_text: This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.

title: Introduction to Sport Engineering
scope: This is an introductory course to impart knowledge and skill set related to working with human in sports engineering application. Understanding human movement pattern and performance measurement. Understand, assess and analyze effect of equipment, sports surfaces and environment on sports performance. Use of ergonomic concepts, image processing, smart sensors and data analysis in sports engineering. Standard techniques of evaluation and testing of sports equipment and sports surfaces and appreciation of business around sports industry. 3. Learning outcome: Course Learning Outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand the fundamentals of human movement and apply engineering principles to analyze sports performance. Appreciate the role of ethics, human factors, and design considerations in sports technology. Utilize modern computing tools for motion analysis and performance evaluation in sports. Gain insights into sports infrastructure, surface design, and their impact on athlete performance. Explore the business, innovation, and marketing potential within the sports ecosystem from an engineering perspective.
description: The course essentially prepares engineering students to utilize their existing technical knowhow for sports applications. The specific topics will include, working with human and human movement patterns, qualitative and quantitative techniques for analysis of human movement. Sports performance measure and analysis. Sports and training equipment case study, business around sports

title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
scope: The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world applications at the micro- and nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces, to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains.
description: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices.

title: Continuum Mechanics
scope: This course will provide an introduction to continuum mechanics. It aims to develop in students the foundational mathematical rigor needed to understand advanced topics in solid and fluid me- chanics.
description: Introduction to tensors, tensor algebra and tensor calculus. Kinematics of deformation (displace- ment, velocity, deformation gradient, material and spatial field descriptions, description of local deformation, linearized kinematics, kinematic rates), left & right Cauchy-Green deformation ten- sor, Cauchy-Lagrangian strain tensor. Traction and stress (first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, second Piola- Kirchhoff stress, Biot stress etc). Mechanical conservation and balance laws (conservation of mass, conservation of linear momentum, conservation of angular momentum, conservation of energy, work done by stresses and the principle of virtual work, BVP, IVP, calculus of variation). Constitutive relations (constraints on constitutive relations, frame indifference, objectivity, material symmetry, constitutive models for linearly elastic, hyperelastic solids and fluid flows).

title: SMART MATERIALS
scope: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.
description: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

scope.supporting_text: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.

description.supporting_text: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

title: Quality Control, Assurance and Reliability
scope: This course presents an exposition to the modern thoughts on quality and related practices. The principles and techniques for quality control, based on statistical methods and the procedures for quality assurance are covered. Tools for quality engineering and quality management are dealt in detail. Concepts of reliability and methods to improve product and systems reliability are also covered. The course is tailored to enable students to become successful managers in a sustained manner, thereby provide support to the business houses in their never-ending quest for quality.
description: Basic concepts of probability and probability distribution, Standard probability distribution, Sampling and Sampling Distributions, Confidence intervals, testing significance, Statistical tolerance, Various types of control charts, Statistical process control techniques, Defect diagnosis and prevention, Basic concepts of reliability, Reliability design evaluation and control, Method of applying total quality management into production process.

title: Mechanism and Robotics
scope: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain.

scope.supporting_text: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain.

title: Finite Element Method
scope: The scope of the course is limited to an introduction to FEA as applied to elasticity problems in solid and structural mechanics. This course will train the students to analyze real-world structural mechanics problems using the finite element method. Students will be introduced to the mathe- matical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software are built. The objectives of the course are: CO1. Understand strong and weak formulations, methods of weighted residuals Rayleigh-Ritz method. CO2. Understand the finite element method procedure, which converts a given boundary value problem into a set of algebraic linear equations that can be solved using computer. CO3. Understand the implementation of FEM for linear analysis of 1D and 2D problems of solid mechanics and heat transfer.
description: Fundamental concepts, matrix algebra and gaussian elimination, one-dimensional problems, trusses, two-dimensional problems using constant strain triangles, axisymmetric solids subjected to ax- isymmetric loading, two-dimensional isoparametric elements and numerical integration, beams and frames, three-dimensional problems in stress analysis, scalar field problems, dynamic con- siderations, pre-processing and post processing.

title: Machine Tool Engineering
scope: The Course is intended to focus the student’s attention on the concepts of design, analysis and features of different types of machine Tools, different machine elements to make a machine tool and new concepts in machine tool engineering. Course Objectives (CO): CLO1. To advance the theoretical and fundamental understanding of machining processes CLO2. To understand the concept of hydraulic and mechanical transmissions employed in machine tools CLO3. Calculation of machining time of various operations CLO4. To understand the design of gear boxes for stepped control of speed and feed in machine tools CLO5. To understand the design solution of different machine tool elements CLO6. To understand the functioning and operation of numerically control machine tools.
description: Design principles of machine tools; stiffness and rigidity of separate construction elements and their combined behaviour under load; design of stepped and stepless drives; electrical, mechanical and hydraulic drives; design of bearings and slideways; machine tool controls; machine tool dynamics; recent developments in machine tool design

title: Deep Neural Networks
scope: This course is designed to impart the knowledge to understand the basics of deep learning and their applications in mechanical engineering. The objectives of this course are: • Understand and explain the architecture, training, and optimization techniques used in deep neural networks. • Apply deep learning techniques to solve problems in mechanical engineering domain. • Analyze the performance and behavior of deep learning models. • Evaluate the strengths and limitations of different deep learning architectures and techniques for mechanical engineering specific problems. • Critically assess the latest advancements in deep learning.
description: Introduction to neural networks, approximation properties, backpropagation, deep network training, regularization and optimization, convolution neural networks, recurrent neural networks, attention models, transformers, neural architecture search, federated learning, meta-learning, applications in time series modeling and forecasting, online (incremental) learning.

title: Industrial Robotics and Controls
scope: This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis, and operation of industrial robotic manipulators. Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems. Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using industrial-grade platforms. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic manipulators. CO2 Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-and- place, assembly, and material handling. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions. _
description: This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics include principles of robot kinematics, statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation and precision assembly; sensor-integrated robotic systems; collaborative robotics; robotic work-cell implementation; and case studies and applications of industrial robots in intelligent manufacturing environments.

title: Moulding Methods for Electronic Components
scope: This course introduces theoretical, analytical, and practical knowledge of plastic materials used in the electronic industry, as well as the manufacturing methods for plastic components. It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies.
description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plastic- moulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components. Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry.

title: Computer Aided Design & Additive Manufacturing
scope: The course aims to develop knowledge and practical skills in advanced CAD, geometric mod- elling, topology optimisation, and additive manufacturing techniques. It enables students to apply geometric modelling, GD&T (ASME Y14.5), generative design, and modern engineering software to design, analyse, and validate innovative and manufacturable engineering products. The course is intended to enable students to:
description: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design (CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation, and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro- duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative, lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products.

description.supporting_text: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design (CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation, and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro- duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative, lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products.

title: Theory of Elasticity & Plasticity
description: The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. The course covers basic theory of elasticity, 2-D and 3-D problems of elasticity, Theories of plastic flow, Flow of ideally plastic and strain hardening metals, and theory of metal forming processes. 2. Course Level Objectives: The course is for higher degree students to prepare them in applying the theory on some problems of practical and design interest. The students will be able to appreciate underlying meaning of material and structural behavior under complex loading conditions. Students are also encouraged to do assignments using the ANSYS/ABAQUS package to solve problems of elasticity and plasticity to compare the analytical solutions. CO1: Understand the concept of stress and strain in situations where large deformations are involved. CO2: Appreciate the governing differential equations that describe a general boundary value problem in elasticity. CO3: Solve the general elasticity boundary value problems with various boundary conditions using methods of complex variable techniques CO4: Appreciate the concept of yielding and yield criteria. Yield surface and normality rule, associated flow rule

title: Micro Fluidics And Its Applications
scope: The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world applications at the micro- and nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces, to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains. Prerequisite: Basic fluid Mechanics understanding
description: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices.

title: SMART MATERIALS
scope: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.
description: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

scope.supporting_text: This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.

description.supporting_text: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

title: Quality Control, Assurance and Reliability
scope: This course presents an exposition to the modern thoughts on quality and related practices. The principles and techniques for quality control, based on statistical methods and the procedures for quality assurance are covered. Tools for quality engineering and quality management are dealt in detail. Concepts of reliability and methods to improve product and systems reliability are also covered. The course is tailored to enable students to become successful managers in a sustained manner, thereby provide support to the business houses in their never-ending quest for quality.
description: Basic concepts of probability and probability distribution, Standard probability distribution, Sampling and Sampling Distributions, Confidence intervals, testing significance, Statistical tolerance, Various types of control charts, Statistical process control techniques, Defect diagnosis and prevention, Basic concepts of reliability, Reliability design evaluation and control, Method of applying total quality management into production process.

title: ADVANCED VLSI DESIGN
scope: The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices. Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages of the design of a modern digital system.
description: The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.

title: Advanced VLSI Architectures
scope: The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The scope of the course covers the following in detail: a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors
description: The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures.

scope.supporting_text: The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The scope of the course covers the following in detail: a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors

description.supporting_text: The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures.

title: Advance Analog and Mixed Signal Design
scope: This course is designed to provide in-depth knowledge and hands-on expertise in designing advanced analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits with a focus on modern CMOS technologies. The course aims to bridge the gap between analog fundamentals and practical design of performance-critical blocks such as Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), oscillators, and Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs). It equips students to analyze, architect, and implement key mixed-signal blocks considering design trade-offs, non-idealities, and layout constraints. Emerging trends such as energy harvesting, sensor interface circuits, and digitally assisted analog systems are also discussed to build readiness for research and industrial innovation.
description: Mixed signal blocks design issues,, design of high resolution, speed Comparators,, design of Active Mixers-balanced/ unbalanced,, Data Converters Architectures, CMOS multipliers , dividers and modulators , filters- active/ passive/ switched capacitor, Signal Conditioning and sensor associated circuits, Frequency Synthesizers, Phase Locked Loop, Power Management Circuits, Integrated Voltage Regulators, Energy Harvesting Circuits, Analog Testing, Analog layouts, noise issues, emerging trendshigh

title: VLSI Fabrication Technology
scope: The objective of the course is not only to introduce the basic principles involved in IC fabrication, but also, to discuss processing technology. Fabrication of integrated circuits is a joint venture by electrical engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges across various disciplines.
description: Historical perspective; Processing overview; Crystallography of semiconductors; Defects in semiconductors; Clean room; Wafer- growth; cleaning; oxidation; epitaxy; wet and dry etching; lithographic process; diffusion; ion implantation; deposition of films using CVD, and PVD techniques; device and circuit fabrication; Process Integration: Passive components, Bipolar Technology and MOSFET Technology, Fabrication of advanced VLSI devices; System on chip; Future trends and Challenges: Laboratory components: Simulation of key fabrication processes using CAD tools; Demonstration of basic FEOL/BEOL fabrication processes; Fabrication and testing of electronic devices.

scope: The objective of this course is to understand the need and importance of digital VLSI design in CMOS integrated circuits. To understand different design principles used in the design of Digital VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS with emphasis on low power and high performance.
description: We will study the fundamental structures of VLSI Systems at the lowest levels of system abstraction, namely those associated with the direct application of VLSI devices to particular problems of interest. The broad topics of coverage includes Principles of operations of CMOS transistors used as a digital switch and various other topologies used in Digital VLSI Design, Logic implementation strategies and performance characterization of the VLSI circuits, Low Power Design, different clocking strategies, symbolic layout systems, CMOS subsystems design and Memory modules.

title: Physics and Modeling of Microelectronic Devices
scope: This course is designed to provide the basic physical concepts behind microelectronic devices and imparts information on modeling of these devices for their use as circuit elements in integrated circuits. It will provide the ability to deal with advanced concepts of microelectronic devices along with non-ideal effects in devices with an attempt to establish an introduction to research methodology.
description: Physics and properties of semiconductor - a review; Semiconductor transport model, modeling of metal-semiconductor junctions, pn homojunction and heterojunctions, bipolar transistor, JFET, MESFET, HEMT and; MOS capacitor, modeling of MOSFET, scaling issues, and recent trends in advanced MOSFETs Laboratory Components: Modeling and simulation of silicon-based devices with TCAD software. I-V, C-V measurement of MS and MOS junctions.

title: DESIGN OF MACHINE ELEMENTS
scope: To prepare a student of mechanical engineering to apply theory and practice of Design of Mechanical Elements. It is an introductory course laying foundation on design ground rules, application of strength of material principles, selection of components, and selection of materials for a given application.
description: The course introduces students to concepts and nuances of Mechanical Engineering Design. Content includes materials, standards and design of machine elements and application of scientific principles, technical knowledge, and imaginative skills to be developed in a student. The machine elements covered are Shafts, Screw fasteners, Welded joints, Springs, Brakes & Clutches, Bearings and Gears. The Tutorial classes of the course will be mainly used for assisted problem solving, consultation and evaluation.

title: AUTOMATION AND CONTROL
scope: This course is intended to a comprehensive knowledge of the technology related to Mechatronics and Automation. The necessity of integrating and embedding electronics and microprocessor into mechanical systems have been long felt, due to rapid progress in microprocessor computer based technology, in domestic products to manufacturing systems. Mechatronics is a recently defined engineering field that builds on the traditional mechanical engineering studies, combines it with technologies from the electrical, electronics, computer and control fields, using techniques such as simultaneous engineering to provide solutions in manufacturing applications. Also, mechatronics has been applied to manufacturing and other industrial automation: robotic automation found in car automated production lines, such as welding, and assembly line in computer integrated manufacture etc. Thus, the manufacturing system is greatly enhanced by the application of mechatronics. This course will develop overall background of the student in interdisciplinary mechatronic technology and a broad introduction to the issues encountered and techniques required in developing mechatronic products and automation systems.

title: Machining and Machine Tools
scope: This course is designed to enrich theoretical, analytical as well as practical knowledge about metal cutting techniques and various machine tools used in manufacturing. The course include undrerstanding of important factors associated with machining such as what is the mechanics of cutting, why cutting fluid is necessary in metal removal, and how abrasive machining processes are different from tool-based cutting processes. The course also includes design aspect of cutting tools, machine parts (structure, spindles, jigs-fixtures) would be explored to comprehend the knowledge of machine tools.
description: Significance of metal machining and machine tools, Geometry of cutting tools, Mechanics of machining processes and analysis, Role of cutting fluids and properties, Abrasive machining processes and analysis, Economics of machining, Regulation of speed and feed rates in machine tools, Design of machine tool structures, Guideways, Spindles, Design of cutting tools for various machine tools, Jigs and Fixtures

scope.supporting_text: This course is designed to enrich theoretical, analytical as well as practical knowledge about metal cutting techniques and various machine tools used in manufacturing. The course include undrerstanding of important factors associated with machining such as what is the mechanics of cutting, why cutting fluid is necessary in metal removal, and how abrasive machining processes are different from tool-based cutting processes. The course also includes design aspect of cutting tools, machine parts (structure, spindles, jigs-fixtures) would be explored to comprehend the knowledge of machine tools.

description.supporting_text: Significance of metal machining and machine tools, Geometry of cutting tools, Mechanics of machining processes and analysis, Role of cutting fluids and properties, Abrasive machining processes and analysis, Economics of machining, Regulation of speed and feed rates in machine tools, Design of machine tool structures, Guideways, Spindles, Design of cutting tools for various machine tools, Jigs and Fixtures

title: Lean Manufacturing
scope: In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from price- cutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business leaders worldwide. With a market capitalization greater than the value of General Motors, Ford and Chrysler combined; Toyota is the world’s most profitable automaker. Toyota’s well known “secret weapon” is lean manufacturing – the revolutionary approach to business processes that it invented in the 1950’s and has spent decades for perfecting. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain competitive advantage. But are they? The course explains Toyota’s unique approach to Lean manufacturing, that drive Toyota’s quality and efficiency obsessed culture. You will valuable insights that can be applied to any organization and any business process, whether in services or manufacturing. You will discover how the right combination of long- term philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning enterprise – the Toyota way. At the end of this course, the students will be able to understand the importance of lean manufacturing / The Toyota Way as a strategic weapon, the students will be able to understand the World –Class power of the Toyota way
description: Fundamentals of continuous improvement, value-added and waste elimination, elements of lean production: small lot production, setup time reduction, maintaining and improving equipment, pull production systems, focused factories and group technologies, work cells and cellular manufacturing, standard operations, quality of design, systems for eliminating defects, simplified production planning and control systems: scheduling for smooth flow, synchronizing and balancing process, planning and control in pull production, beyond the production systems: managing the supply chain, activity based costing, performance measurement.

title: Supply Chain Modelling and Empirical Analysis
scope: The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insight into the application of various supply chain modelling approaches and empirical analysis for evidence driven decision making in supply chain. The objectives of the course are: • To introduce concept of decision making on the basis of multiple experts’ opinion on various different supply chain problems, practices and strategies. • To develop skill sets to analyze the qualitative data with a focus on empirical modelling for data driven decisions in supply chain. • To develop model for life cycle analysis for measuring environmental sustainability in supply chain. • To understand and analyse the various aspects of digital supply chain, cultural implications and their impact on supply chain performance.

title: INNOVATION AND DESIGN THINKING
scope: The objective is to develop knowhow and skills that promote human-centered approach to innovation through design thinking (DT). It will aim to develop understanding of consumer needs & using creativity for new ideas/products (or re-design products) for solving problems. Course will also help understand prototyping, testing of new ideas & see the context of the larger ecosystem. Focus will be on understanding design thinking concept and tools for effective innovations that can solve consumers’ needs holistically. Design Thinking process is laid across 3 stages- inspiration, ideation and implementation for new product development or re-design & concepts like MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem will be also covered. The pedagogical focus will be on hands-on approach to learning.
description: Human-centered innovation, Design thinking (DT), consumer needs, creativity for new ideas/products (or re- design products) for solving problems, DT process’ stages– inspiration, ideation & implementation, DT tools – stakeholder map, user persona, Hook’s canvas, empathy map, AEIOU model, PoV, problem statement, stakeholder wish list, SCAMPER, prototyping & testing, MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem. The pedagogical focus will be on hands-on approach to learning.

title: Managerial Economics
scope: This course aims at providing an overview of comprehensive coverage of fundamental concepts, analytical tools understanding economics of business decision making for a profitable and sustainable status in dynamic business environment. While the primary unit of analysis is firm, the coverage of this course would enable finding & understanding connections of firms’ decisions with its industry and the macroeconomic environment at large.
description: The course provides to the students: 1. An insight into the scientific & analytical methods, techniques and tools of economics 2. A precise and comprehensive coverage of fundamental concepts in economics 3. Suitable real world applications & examples to expose him/her to possibilities of implementing concepts in business and economic practices and polices 4. Approach to integrate different aspects of a firm’s economic decisions within the firm’s framework as well as find & understand connections with the macroeconomic environment

title: Marketing
scope: On successful completion of this course, participants will be able to critically analyze and intelligently draw inference about the marketing strategies of organizations. Through an intensive assignment an effort will be made to develop the necessary skills for crafting a typical marketing plan grounded in real world data. Finally, awareness of tools available to marketing managers to facilitate planning and decision-making would be one of the gains from the course. Students are encouraged to bring some of the topical issues of contemporary concern in marketing to the classroom for discussion. Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a group marketing project assignment.
description: This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating, communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions.

Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a group marketing project assignment.

description.supporting_text: This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating, communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions.

title: Statistics & Basic Econometrics
scope: This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R.
description: Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in this course.

scope.supporting_text: This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R.

description.supporting_text: Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in this course.

description: This course introduces students to the practical usage of databases, emphasizing SQL. As big data problems become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. Students will learn how to extract valuable insights from databases through data analytics powered by SQL.

title: Programming for Analytics
scope: 1. To develop proficiency in programming to automate analytical workflows, including data cleaning, transformation, and report generation, reducing manual effort and increasing accuracy. 2. To gain hands-on experience with programming tools and libraries (e.g., Python’s pandas, R’s tidyverse) to efficiently process, manipulate, and analyze large and complex datasets beyond the capabilities of traditional tools. 3. To apply programming best practices to ensure reproducibility, and transparency, for analytical processes, enabling consistent validation and collaboration across teams.
description: Variables & data types, operators, conditional statements, iteration statements, functions, Objects, and classes for Python; Data structures – vectors, matrices, lists, tuples, dictionaries, data frames, Packages: using existing packages and creating new packages, Data loading: from CSV, MS Excel, JSON & SQL databases Data wrangling: describing, summarizing, manipulating, and handling missing values of data in data frames; perform an operation such as delete values, find unique values, drop duplicate values, grouping, and performing loop operations over columns or rows; merging data frames; handling categorical data; handling time-series data, handling text data, web scraping, and handling images. Basics of version control using Github. Primary languages are R and Python.

title: Deep Learning for Business
scope: The course aims to equip students with foundational and practical knowledge of deep learning algorithms and their applications in solving business challenges. The course emphasizes: a. Understanding core deep learning architectures and techniques b. Translating business problems into machine learning tasks c. Developing, training, and tuning deep learning models using appropriate tools d. Applying deep learning to solve business challenges e. Utilizing TensorFlow and Keras libraries on Google Colab to implement and explore deep learning algorithms f. Recognizing the limitations, ethical concerns, and interpretability issues of deep models in business decision-making g. Engaging in a group-based project, where students apply deep learning techniques to some real- world business problems
description: This course offers an introduction to deep learning and its practical relevance in business contexts. It covers foundational concepts such as neural networks, linear and logistic regression using neural architectures, deep neural networks, hyperparameter tuning, and advanced models like CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs, GANs, and deep reinforcement learning. The course blends theoretical understanding with hands-on applications to solve real-world business problems. It also highlights the challenges and limitations of deep learning methods in practice.
makeup_policy: No extensions shall be granted for projects. Genuine cases such as hospitalization (upon production of the relevant documents/proof) will be considered upon discussion with individuals/team for any make ups for the final Exam.

title: PRESCRIPTIVE ANALYTICS WITH MATHEMATICAL
scope: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post- mortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making. Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary Prescriptive analytics assists the decision-maker in identifying the best action (optimal solution) given the problem context. The difference between decisions made using descriptive/predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics is that a prescriptive analytics algorithm seeks the best decision (optimal solution) based on an objective function (sometimes multiple objective functions) and a set of constraints. Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era. Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. Students can download a trial version (free) of Lingo from https://www.lindo.com/index.php/products/lingo-and-optimization-modeling Using Lingo, large-scale, complex Prescriptive Analytics problems can be solved.

scope.supporting_text: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post- mortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making.
