title: MARKETING ANALYTICS
description: (Scope and Objective): This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods, and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence, analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling. Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience, retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks, and optimization. The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics, recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX, and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights, evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels, and brands.

source.supporting_text: (Scope and Objective): This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods, and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence, analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling. Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience, retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks, and optimization. The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics, recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX, and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights, evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels, and brands.

scope: The objectives of this course are: (1) To make you acquainted with the concept of pricing and how data can help in setting the right price for the organization. This will be done primarily through lectures, class discussions and assigned readings.
description: This course provides an introduction to both the theory and the practice of revenue management and pricing, Fundamentals of price theory, Segmentation and price differentiation, Break- even analysis, Price sensitivity and willingness-to-pay, Empirical estimations of price-response functions, Price optimization, Markdown optimization, The hedonic pricing model, Revenue Management, Monte Carlo simulation for pricing decisions, Conjoint analysis for pricing decisions.

title: Marketing Research & Metrics
scope: To impart necessary foundational concepts, methodologies and tools/techniques for role of a market researcher. That role envisages generation of actionable, reliable and accurate information to identify various marketing problems viz. demand forecasting, segmentation, targeting, positioning, new product development etc. and find their effective solutions.
description: All organizations need to research their markets periodically and employ various elements of marketing research process viz. problem definition, development of an approach to the problem, research design formulation, fieldwork & data collection, data preparation & analysis and finally report preparation and presentation. The emphasis of the course is proportionately focused on foundational concepts, methodology & techniques, and marketing research applications. A number of cases will be assigned for discussion in the class. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” and a project assignment in this course characterizes this orientation.

title: Financial Analytics
scope: This course aims at discussing the role of data and analytics in financial decision making, understanding the statistical properties of financial data. The student should be able to price different securities by understanding their characteristics and using different statistical and machine learning techniques. The student should also be able to create optimal portfolios catering to the requirements of different user groups and evaluate the portfolios using different metrics. The course also aims to discuss some of the most prominent applications of Analytics in Finance like Credit Scoring, Debt collection, Sentiment Analysis, Trading strategies

title: Financial Modelling and Valuation
scope: A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed to make thoughtful decisions on company value. This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies. We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company. This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who would like to do so. The course also has a broader appeal to people who want to improve their InstructionDivision knowledge of financial analysis and discover how companies produce and quantify value for theirinvestors. 2. Format: This is a fairly challenging and ambitious course by design. We will use case studies and problem-solving techniques because the course objectives are grounded on the practical application of academic ideas. There will be lectures and discussions throughout class time. The readings will be integrated into the lectures' analytic principles, which will provide a helpful framework for a deeper comprehension of the instances. Please keep in mind that the goal of a valuation exercise is to use a series of techniques and logical steps that represent the complexityof thesituation,notto get it "precise."

title: People Analytics
scope: People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations. However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability. The learning objectives of the course are as under:  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. _ Instruction Division  The student will develop an understanding of the role and importance of HR analytics, and the ability to track, store, retrieve, analyze and interpret HR data to support decision making.  The student will know about the standard HR metrics to measure various facets of HR related outputs and about indices and metrics to measure them.  Employ appropriate software to record, maintain, retrieve and analyze human resources information (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information).  Apply quantitative and qualitative analysis to understand trends and indicators in human resource data; understand and apply various statistical analysis methods.  Apply descriptive and predictive analytics techniques to address HR related issues and make data driven decision making.  Demonstrate how to connect HR results to business results.
description: There will be three weekly classes. Class time will be devoted to lectures, role-plays, exercises, questionnaire, case discussions and videotapes. Lectures will provide analytical concepts that will integrate the readings and serve as useful framework for a richer understanding of cases and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this course. These participative activities are further enhanced by rigorous self-review (through Journal, Follow-up Report and Critique). Tests and Project will provide an opportunity to test comprehension of the theory and readings.

title: Supply Chain Modelling and Empirical Analysis
scope: The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insight into the application of various supply chain modelling approaches and empirical analysis for evidence driven decision making in supply chain. The objectives of the course are: • To introduce concept of decision making on the basis of multiple experts’ opinion on various different supply chain problems, practices and strategies. • To develop skill sets to analyze the qualitative data with a focus on empirical modelling for data driven decisions in supply chain. • To develop model for life cycle analysis for measuring environmental sustainability in supply chain. • To understand and analyse the various aspects of digital supply chain, cultural implications and their impact on supply chain performance.
makeup_policy: No students will be allowed to take make up without prior permission. For the case study and assignment / article/class presentation, no make ups will be granted.

title: Pharmaceutical Analysis
scope: The objective of this course is to provide students with knowledge of basic principles of quantitative analytical chemistry necessary for use and interpretation of pharmaceutical methods of analysis especially those methods official in the Indian, United States and British Pharmacopoeias.
description: Basic techniques of pharmaceutical analysis, data handling and analysis, sources of error in analysis. The analytical methods would comprise various titrimetric methods, such as acid-base, complexometric, non-aqueous, oxidation-reduction, precipitation, conductometric; physical and instrumental analysis such as gravimetric, polarography, nephelometry, amperometry, turbidometry, potentiometry; chromatographic separations such as TLC, column, ion-exchange, extraction methods such as gel-filtration, fractionation processes, analysis of metallic and non-metallic elements; water content, as well as evaluation of drug constituents in various pharmaceutical preparation.
makeup_policy: Make-up is not given as a routine and is considered for only regular students. It is solely dependent on the "genuineness" of the circumstance under which a student fails to appear in a scheduled evaluation component. The students must discuss such a situation with the IC and get prior permission for make-up. In case of urgent medical emergencies, the students must ensure that the message reaches IC as soon as possible. It is particularly difficult to arrange make-up for the lab sessions due to the limited availability of lab instructors who are Ph.D. scholars. Reasonable attendance in theory and practical sessions will be a decisive factor in allowing make-up. The decision of the IC in all matters shall be final.

title: Biological Chemistry
scope: The aim of this course is to describe and explain all biochemical processes of living organisms and their interactions with their networking both in health and disease conditions.
description: This course focuses upon the physiological and medical significance of important biomolecules along with their use as drug targets. The course also elaborates the role of vitamins as prosthetic groups of enzymes and enzyme kinetics and regulation. The course deals with the understanding of chemical structures, biochemical reactions metabolic pathways related to carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and protein synthesis and diseases arising from defects in these pathways.

There is no makeup for continuous evaluation.

title: Pharmacology-I
scope: This course is intended to impart the knowledge regarding the sources, routes of drug administration, pharmacokinetics (ADME) and phramacodynamics (mechanism of action) of various drugs. This course is also intended to impart the knowledge regarding the concepts of action of drugs on various systems of the human body including ANS, SNS and CNS. The course also deals with therapeutic uses, side effects and contraindications of the drugs, which are commonly prescribed for the treatment of various disease conditions.

title: PHARMACEUTICAL FORMULATIONS II
scope: It is a course intended to give students insight into the problems involved in making drug dosage forms. It brings together the various sciences involved in developing pharmaceutical product formulations and evaluating their quality. The laboratory component involves some fundamental exercises in the evolution of products such as tablets, ointments, solutions, parenteral products, sustained-action medications, etc. It also imparts knowledge of newer dosage forms.
description: Physical, chemical, and biopharmaceutical considerations in formulations, absorption, distribution, and elimination of drugs; pharmaceutical additives; formulation, manufacturing, packaging, quality control, and stability of solid dosage forms, semi-solid dosage forms, liquids dosage forms, and sterile preparations including parenteral suspensions, emulsions, depot formulations; microencapsulation and controlled release formulations; targeted drug delivery systems; multi-unit particulate systems; transdermal, gastroretentive, and nasopulmonary drug delivery systems; aerosol products and packaging.

title: PARENTERAL PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT
scope: This course will provide overview on parenteral product development & designed for students to understand critical aspect of parenteral product development and manufacturing. This course covers basic information, understanding and application of key operations followed during parenteral product manufacturing like lyophilization, aseptic processing, & filtration along with Quality Assurance, control & packaging requirement. This course also covers regulatory consideration for parenteral product assessment with respect to safety for intended application.
description: B Introduction to parenteral product & their types, products characteristics; Vehicles requirement for Parenteral Products manufacturing; Formulation & process consideration for development of parenteral products; Introduction & understanding of various aspects of unit operation in parenteral product manufacturing; Critical Quality attributes of Parenteral Product; Various Sterilization techniques for parenteral products; Understanding of key requirements for aseptic processing; Understanding of Lyophilization techniques of stable product development; Regulatory consideration for safety assessment of Parenteral Products; Packaging requirement for Parenteral Drug Products; Regulatory perspective for Complex Injectable products development and filing.
makeup_policy: A student may apply for the makeup if he/she is not able to attend regular midsemester and comprehensive exams due to genuine exigencies. No makeup request will be accepted for quizzes and other continuous assessment component.

title: Immunopharmacology
scope: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong learning and career development.

scope.supporting_text: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong learning and career development.

title: Modern Pharmaceutical Analytical Techniques
description: This course is a laboratory oriented course and covers various analytical aspects like principles of sample preparation, method development for analysis and characterization of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) and formulations, using techniques such as High Performance Liquid chromatography (HPLC), bio- chromatography, size exclusion, affinity, chiral, fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC). Characterization of nanopharmaceutcials using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) techniques. 1H and 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in structural characterization, Mass Spectrometry and its applications, Elemental analysis, Optical, chiro-optical techniques in structure elucidation. 2. Scope of the Course: The course is aimed at exposing the students to modern analytical techniques in relevance to pharmaceutical industries. Training with respect to the handling and operation of sophisticated instruments, interpretation of results obtained for the characterization of molecules, their qualitative and quantitative evaluation are emphasized. Objectives of the Course: Exposure to principles, instrumentation, calibration and operation of analytical instruments. Obtaining spectral data, their interpretation, evaluation of qualitative and quantitative aspects of drugs and their estimation.

title: Computer Aided Drug Design
scope: To develop an appreciation of inter- and intra- molecular energies and forces. To introduce the techniques of computational chemistry and to demonstrate their application to the design of drugs. To demonstrate the use of simulation as an alternative to experimental work. On completion the student should be aware of the scope and limitations of the various theoretical and computational tools available to the pharmaceutical scientist and of the application of these techniques in the design of novel drugs. The student will also have gained insight into the practical implementation of the methods of molecular and bio-molecular modeling.
description: 3D structure and function of bio-molecules; targets of drugs and design principles; molecular modeling methodologies; quantitative structure-activity relationships; chemical compound databases and search tools; interactive graphics in drug design; molecular surfaces and algorithm of automated docking of drugs into receptor sites; receptor mapping; introduction to molecular modeling and docking software.
makeup_policy: Generally, make-up will be considered for regular students only and make-up's are not given as a routine. It is solely dependent on the "genuineness" of the circumstance under which a student fails to appear in a scheduled evaluation component. However, the make-up application should be personally given to Instructor-in-Charge and not slipped into the chamber of the Instructor-in-Charge.

scope.supporting_text: To develop an appreciation of inter- and intra- molecular energies and forces. To introduce the techniques of computational chemistry and to demonstrate their application to the design of drugs. To demonstrate the use of simulation as an alternative to experimental work. On completion the student should be aware of the scope and limitations of the various theoretical and computational tools available to the pharmaceutical scientist and of the application of these techniques in the design of novel drugs. The student will also have gained insight into the practical implementation of the methods of molecular and bio-molecular modeling.

description.supporting_text: 3D structure and function of bio-molecules; targets of drugs and design principles; molecular modeling methodologies; quantitative structure-activity relationships; chemical compound databases and search tools; interactive graphics in drug design; molecular surfaces and algorithm of automated docking of drugs into receptor sites; receptor mapping; introduction to molecular modeling and docking software.

title.supporting_text: Course Title : Computer Aided Drug Design

title: Advanced Physical Pharmaceutics
scope: Prior to the development of any dosage form with a new or old drug candidate, it is essential that certain fundamental physical and chemical properties of the drug molecule and other derived properties of the drug are determined. This information dictates possible approaches in formulation development. The aim of this course is to make the students understand those physicochemical principles which must be applied in the formulation and development of an efficacious dosage form, so that required duration and intensity of effect can be ensured at the intended site of action.
description: Physicochemical principles involved in effective formulation development, including various aspects like, pharmaceutical preformulation including bulk characteristics, polymorphism, solubility analysis, solid and solution state stability, compatibility. This course also cover various ICH guidelines like stability study, specifications, impurities which are required during formulation development. This course also discussed details about mechanical properties of powders, principles of dissolution, in-vitro in-vivo correlation (IVIVC), polymer science, etc.

title: CLINICAL RESEARCH
scope: There is a growing need for clinical researchers in the health industries (pharmaceutical, biotechnology/medical device companies, research institutes, and hospitals) involved in the development of new drugs and therapies. This course is aimed at training students in conducting clinical trials on humans with new drugs/therapies before they are introduced to the market. Students completing the coursework will gain specialized knowledge and skills required to design, monitor, and manage clinical trials. Courses include the drug development process; regulations, guidelines, and standards; research methodology and biostatistics; clinical trial organization, monitoring, and documentation; and project management.
description: Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board; regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP); related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study design; trial development (protocol, case report form, and data management); clinical trial management- coordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology, implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report preparation for various submissions.
makeup_policy: Generally, make-up will be considered for regular students only.

title: Pharmacokinetics & Clinical Pharmacy
scope: The course imparts knowledge of pharmacokinetics, its application, pharmacokinetic studies, mathematical modeling, and experimental design. This will help students to gain knowledge in a very important area of pharmacy. Practicals are designed to expose students to pharmacokinetic studies.
description: Introduction to pharmacokinetic modeling of drugs; Compartmental modeling including one compartmental and two compartmental models; Non-compartmental analysis (NCA); Bioequivalence and comparative bioavailability studies; Pharmacokinetic Pharmacodynamic modeling techniques, determination of order of absorption and absorption rate constant by Wagner-Nelson method; non-linear pharmacokinetics; Pharmacokinetic drug interactions; multi-dose pharmacokinetics of drugs following one compartmental model; Design of multi-dose regimen; Dosage regimen adjustment in renal impairment; Application of the pharmacokinetic principles for better therapeutic outcomes

title: Pharmaceutical Biotechnology
scope: The course deals with the principles and techniques of biotechnology with direct application in the field of pharmaceutical sciences. It aims at bringing together the principles of molecular biology, molecular genetics, biochemical engineering, protein engineering, enzymtechnology, bio- informatics required to develop a successful biotechnology based pharmaceutical product. The applications of genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, hybridoma technology, transgenic animals, gene therapy, drug delivery aspects of biotechnology products and their clinical evaluation are also dealt with in this course.

title: Pharmaceutical Administration & Management (PAM)
scope: The objective of the course is to help students understand new drug and product considerations and planning; strategic considerations; project implementation; product development; production management & scale-up; marketing strategy; human resources development; ethical issues; and R&D management.
description: This course introduces students to various organizational aspects, focusing on pharmaceutical management. Topics include technology innovation, drug planning, strategy, project execution, product development, production, scale-up, marketing, IPR, HR, industrial relations, documentation, R&D, and ethics.

title: Advanced Drug Delivery Systems
scope: The prime objective of this course is to impart knowledge of design, development and evaluation of novel drug delivery systems (NDDS). The primary focus would be on integrating the biopharmaceutical, physiochemical and physiological properties for design and development of (NDDS) with due consideration of pharmacological action. Excipients used in design and development of NDDS would be covered exhaustively.
description: A study of physicochemical and biopharmaceutical factors involved in the design of novel drug delivery systems like mucosal, particulate systems for systemic delivery of bioactive molecules. Special considerations for delivery of protein, peptide and other biological products. In vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel drug delivery systems

title: Retrosynthetic Analysis
scope: Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic Analysis. At the end of the course, students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug molecules with appropriate justification.
description: This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course.

scope: The objective of this course is to understand the principles of experimental pharmacology with special emphasis on in-vitro cell culture techniques and in vivo experimentation. Basics of animal handling, breeding, diet manipulation, dose Calculation-Human equivalent dose, development of new animal models and evaluation techniques for various diseases and their standardization will be covered. The course also includes toxicological, teratogenic, carcinogenic studies, and data analysis

title: Pharmaceutical Applications of Polymers and Biopolymers
scope: This course includes the analysis of polymers and biopolymers at a molecular scale, and design of devices used in contact with biological systems. Topics include molecular interactions between bio- and synthetic molecules and surfaces; design, synthesis, and processing approaches for materials that control cell functions; and application of state-of-the-art materials science to problems in tissue engineering, drug delivery, vaccines, and cell-guiding surfaces. This course covers the fundamental concepts (physical chemistry, chemistry, and materials physics, and biology) behind the design at a molecular scale of synthetic materials with biological functions.

title: Classical Mechanics
scope: To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics, including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity.
description: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles, central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in inertial, and rotating reference frames.
makeup_policy: No make-up for tutorial tests. For midterm/comprehensive exam, make up will be granted to genuine cases after proper verification (case-by-case basis).

(Hysteresis Loop) ferromagnetic material • Determine retentivity and coercivity from the magnetic hysteresis loop • Investigate the effect of an external magnetic field Measurement of Magneto- on the resistivity of materials 10 resistance • Measure the magneto-resistance of a semiconductor crystal • Study the magnetic field produced by a current- carrying conductor 11 Biot–Savart Law • Experimentally verify the Biot–Savart law of electromagnetism • Measure the force experienced by a current- carrying conductor in a magnetic field Current Balance 12 • Verify the Lorentz force and the principle of electromagnetic induction Important Instructions to the students: 1. Day-to-day performance would carry 20 (15 for Performing Experiments, completing results/graphs and calculations, and submitting in stipulated time and 5 for viva) marks for each experiment. 2. We will take the best (N-1) experiments (where N is the total number of experiments performed by a particular Section during the semester) while doing the evaluation at the end of the semester. Total marks for day-to-day performance would be scaled down to 80 marks. 3. There will be 4 lectures delivered by the Lab instructors which are mandatory to attend. At the end of each lecture, there will be a short quiz of 5 marks based on the topics discussed in the lecture. These 20 marks will be added to day-to-day performance. 4. Students would perform 1 experiment per turn and upload the calculations and the results on the Google Classroom before the next turn (6 days) in the prescribed format. If they fail to do so, 1 mark per day post deadline would be STRICTLY deducted from day-to-day performance for that experiment, and after 3 days post deadline the experiment WILL NOT be evaluated. 5. Students are expected to read about the allotted experiments from the manuals before coming to the Lab. Viva for each experiment will be conducted on the same day of the experiment. 6. The Lab Report should be written in the prescribed format only. It should contain the scanned copy of the hand written calculation with your NAME and ID. Similarly the graphs/ plots in the report should also contain your NAME and ID, so that they can be authenticated as genuine. In addition to the lab Report, merge the scanned copy of the relevant Observation Sheet and submit it as a single Pdf file only. The name of that Pdf file should be <Your Name_Name of The Experiment.pdf>. 7. Students are expected to maintain discipline during the lab hours. 8. As each lab is an evaluative component, mobile phones and any other electronic gadgets are strictly prohibited during lab hours. If found, students will be asked to leave the lab and will be given zero for that experiment. Responsibilities of the students: 1. To carry his/her valid identity card issued by the institute. 2. To arrive at the laboratory in time. 3. To get one reading in the observation table verified and attested by the instructors. 4. To understand and strictly follow the safety precautions.

title: QUANTUM MECHANICS II
scope: ● Quantum theory of angular momentum. ● Three-Dimensional Problems in Quantum Mechanics, Central Potential problem ● Time independent approximation methods in quantum mechanics ● Quantum mechanics of time-dependent systems and quantum theory of scattering.
description: This course is the second of the two-semesters course on Quantum Mechanics and is a continuation of Quantum Mechanics I. In this course we will discuss quantum theory of angular momentum and addition of angular momentum, applications to spherically symmetric potential, approximation methods to time independent systems, and time dependent systems.

title: STATISTICAL MECHANICS
scope: ❖ Develop familiarity with the basic techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics. ❖ Understand the role of probability theory and statistics in relating microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of thermodynamic systems ❖ Learn key methods of ensemble theory ❖ Distinguish between quantum and classical statistical mechanics and compute essential properties of ideal Bosonic and Fermionic systems.
description: This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems. Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves. In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions.

title: Computational Physics
scope: The objective of the course is to develop a practical understanding of the basic numerical methods used to obtain approximate solutions of mathematical problems arising in physics. Emphasis will be placed on the hands-on construction of elementary algorithms, the translation of equations into finite computational procedures, and the interpretation and validation of numerical results. Students will also learn to use scientific programming and visualization tools, including Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, for studying relevant physical systems.
description: The course introduces elementary computational methods for obtaining approximate solutions to mathematical problems arising in physics. Topics include root finding, systems of linear equations, numerical quadrature, ordinary and partial differential equations, Monte Carlo simulation, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Emphasis will be placed on the hands-on implementation of basic algorithms and their application to representative physical systems.

title: Particle Physics
scope: The above description conveys the scope and objective in great detail.
description: (Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics, providing context for the questions it addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a fair idea of what particle physics is all about and what to expect from this course. The titles of paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the course.) Bright blue sky: What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics? 1. What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the Universe? 2. What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural hierarchy we see at different levels? 3. What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above questions? 4. Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the answers we know? Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle Physics. Relativity + Quantum Mechanics = Quantum Field Theory: Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them. From relativistic quantum mechanics to scattering cross-sections and decay rate: Answers to questions 1 and 2 have been the content of the latter half of your Nuclear and Particle Physics course. The focus of this course would be essentially on questions 3 and 4. It turns out that we know a lot about the fundamental particles and their interactions. In the first module, we will primarily focus on calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates. To do this, we will quickly recap the special theory of relativity (module 1) and the time-dependent perturbation theory (module 2). In Module 2, we will also discuss the relativistic quantum mechanics of spin-0 particles (the Klein-Gordon equation). Module-3 will introduce spin-1/2 particles (Dirac equation) and apply them to classic scattering cross-section calculations in quantum electrodynamics at lowest order in perturbation theory. You will see the famous Feynman diagrams and Feynman rules in action.. We will have some fun with what one can do with the rules, and that is calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates, which experimentalists can actually measure. Indiscreet fall of the discrete symmetries: Symmetry transformations can be continuous or discrete. Discrete symmetries are essentially invariances under a discrete transformation and will be the subject of module-4. Their examples are parity (P) (inversion about origin, i.e., changing x,y,z to -x,-y,-z), time reversal (T) (changing t to -t), and charge conjugation (C) (changing particles to antiparticles and vice versa). Naively, Physics was expected to be invariant under each of these discrete transformations separately. However, it turns out that individually, each of them is violated. In fact, the so-called CPT theorem states that any Lorentz-invariant local quantum field theory with a Hermitian Hamiltonian must be invariant under the combined transformation of Charge conjugation (C), Parity (P), and Time reversal (T). It turns out that the weak interactions violate all three (C, P, and T) and also the combination CP. However, the combined CPT transformation is so far known to be an exact symmetry and any violation of CPT would signal a fundamental trouble either in quantum mechanics or relativity or local interactions. The Story of the separate violations of C, P, and T is intricately tied to the story of weak interaction and will be covered in module 5. Building the Universe from scratch - the blocks and the glue: Module-6 would be the last module of the course and will answer question number 4 in the affirmative and offer a convincing discourse on the same. Until the advent of Particle Physics in the 20th century, symmetries and conservation laws largely served a utilitarian purpose of bookkeeping. Conservation laws offer our first shot at dynamics without having to confront the dynamics head-on. Just look at the stuff before and after a dynamical event, and if conservation laws are applicable, we can pull out the unknown energy or momentum by a straightforward bookkeeping of conserved quantum numbers. However, during the latter half of the 20th century, we learnt that the symmetries aren’t just utilitarian. They are the rhyme and the reason behind why things are the way they are. What do you need to build the Universe from scratch? The bricks (fundamental particles), the cement (glue to bind them to form bound states), and a blueprint (the Lagrangian). All of these and much more are a consequence of some symmetry principles which can be broadly divided into two categories -- spacetime symmetries (Lorentz or, strictly speaking, Poincaré symmetries), and internal or local gauge symmetries. So the question of kinematics, or why the fundamental particles of different mass and spin exist at all, is answered by the spacetime symmetries. Particles of different mass and spin exist as representations of Poincare group. On the other hand, the question of the existence of three different fundamental interactions (excluding gravity for the moment) is answered by the "internal" local gauge symmetries. They are "internal" in the sense that they operate in an abstract internal space different from the "external" spacetime. All the fundamental interactions are explained within the overarching theme of gauge theories. How to break a symmetry without actually breaking it? A massive question: If you think the question is an oxymoron and with a blatant misuse of adjectives, please bear with me until the mist clears. We now have the basic building blocks (particles) and the glue (interactions) which bind them in place as a consequence of spacetime (Poincaré) and internal (Gauge) symmetries. But what is the origin of the mass of the particles? It turns out that you cannot just put a mass term in your fundamental Lagrangian by hand and get on with the business. The question of mass is intricately tied to the question of Lorentz invariance and gauge invariance, and will be covered in the latter half of module 6. In a jigsaw puzzle, each piece is constrained by the shape of the neighbouring pieces. We cannot accommodate mass without fundamentally tweaking the particle content and introducing a "subtle breaking" of the gauge symmetries. There are three different ways in which a symmetry can be broken: explicit, spontaneous, and anomalous (beyond the scope of the course). It turns out that putting a mass term by hand explicitly breaks the local gauge symmetry, and that is nothing short of a sacrilege in particle physics. We can nevertheless break it through the "back door", that is, break it spontaneously! Our Lagrangian, equations of motion, commutation relations, and Feynman rules all respect gauge symmetry, and yet, the choice of a ground state violates the symmetry. Spontaneous symmetry breaking may appear mysterious, but it is rather common. The most famous example is that of a ferromagnet. Its Hamiltonian is invariant under rotational symmetry. This is why, above a critical temperature called the Curie temperature, thanks to thermal agitation, all the spin dipoles are randomly oriented and hence the net magnetization averages out to zero. However, below the Curie temperature, all dipoles spontaneously align in a specific direction, giving non-zero net magnetization. The Hamiltonian is still rotationally invariant, and yet magnetic dipoles select a specific direction and align. It turns out that to realize such spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics, we need to add a spin-0 field and its accompanying dynamics. How exactly the machinery of the Higgs mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking end up endowing fundamental particles with mass cannot be elaborated here. It is said that the proof of the pudding is in eating. We hope to get this far and discuss these issues. Dark Clouds: We started with bright blue skies and end with dark clouds. I wish I could end this preface on a positive

Thus, we use extremely high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them. The focus of this course would be essentially on questions 3 and 4. It turns out that we know a lot about the fundamental particles and their interactions. In the first module, we will primarily focus on calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates. To do this, we will quickly recap the special theory of relativity (module 1) and the time-dependent perturbation theory (module 2). In Module 2, we will also discuss the relativistic quantum mechanics of spin-0 particles (the Klein-Gordon equation). Module-3 will introduce spin-1/2 particles (Dirac equation) and apply them to classic scattering cross-section calculations in quantum electrodynamics at lowest order in perturbation theory. You will see the famous Feynman diagrams and Feynman rules in action.. We will have some fun with what one can do with the rules, and that is calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates, which experimentalists can actually measure. Indiscreet fall of the discrete symmetries: Symmetry transformations can be continuous or discrete. Discrete symmetries are essentially invariances under a discrete transformation and will be the subject of module-4. Their examples are parity (P) (inversion about origin, i.e., changing x,y,z to -x,-y,-z), time reversal (T) (changing t to -t), and charge conjugation (C) (changing particles to antiparticles and vice versa). Naively, Physics was expected to be invariant under each of these discrete transformations separately. However, it turns out that individually, each of them is violated. In fact, the so-called CPT theorem states that any Lorentz-invariant local quantum field theory with a Hermitian Hamiltonian must be invariant under the combined transformation of Charge conjugation (C), Parity (P), and Time reversal (T). It turns out that the weak interactions violate all three (C, P, and T) and also the combination CP. However, the combined CPT transformation is so far known to be an exact symmetry and any violation of CPT would signal a fundamental trouble either in quantum mechanics or relativity or local interactions. The Story of the separate violations of C, P, and T is intricately tied to the story of weak interaction and will be covered in module 5. Building the Universe from scratch - the blocks and the glue: Module-6 would be the last module of the course and will answer question number 4 in the affirmative and offer a convincing discourse on the same. Until the advent of Particle Physics in the 20th century, symmetries and conservation laws largely served a utilitarian purpose of bookkeeping. Conservation laws offer our first shot at dynamics without having to confront the dynamics head-on. Just look at the stuff before and after a dynamical event, and if conservation laws are applicable, we can pull out the unknown energy or momentum by a straightforward bookkeeping of conserved quantum numbers. However, during the latter half of the 20th century, we learnt that the symmetries aren’t just utilitarian. They are the rhyme and the reason behind why things are the way they are. What do you need to build the Universe from scratch? The bricks (fundamental particles), the cement (glue to bind them to form bound states), and a blueprint (the Lagrangian). All of these and much more are a consequence of some symmetry principles which can be broadly divided into two categories -- spacetime symmetries (Lorentz or, strictly speaking, Poincaré symmetries), and internal or local gauge symmetries. So the question of kinematics, or why the fundamental particles of different mass and spin exist at all, is answered by the spacetime symmetries. Particles of different mass and spin exist as representations of Poincare group. On the other hand, the question of the existence of three different fundamental interactions (excluding gravity for the moment) is answered by the "internal" local gauge symmetries. They are "internal" in the sense that they operate in an abstract internal space different from the "external" spacetime. All the fundamental interactions are explained within the overarching theme of gauge theories. How to break a symmetry without actually breaking it? A massive question: If you think the question is an oxymoron and with a blatant misuse of adjectives, please bear with me until the mist clears. We now have the basic building blocks (particles) and the glue (interactions) which bind them in place as a consequence of spacetime (Poincaré) and internal (Gauge) symmetries. But what is the origin of the mass of the particles? It turns out that you cannot just put a mass term in your fundamental Lagrangian by hand and get on with the business. The question of mass is intricately tied to the question of Lorentz invariance and gauge invariance, and will be covered in the latter half of module 6. In a jigsaw puzzle, each piece is constrained by the shape of the neighbouring pieces. We cannot accommodate mass without fundamentally tweaking the particle content and introducing a "subtle breaking" of the gauge symmetries. There are three different ways in which a symmetry can be broken: explicit, spontaneous, and anomalous (beyond the scope of the course). It turns out that putting a mass term by hand explicitly breaks the local gauge symmetry, and that is nothing short of a sacrilege in particle physics. We can nevertheless break it through the "back door", that is, break it spontaneously! Our Lagrangian, equations of motion, commutation relations, and Feynman rules all respect gauge symmetry, and yet, the choice of a ground state violates the symmetry. Spontaneous symmetry breaking may appear mysterious, but it is rather common. The most famous example is that of a ferromagnet. Its Hamiltonian is invariant under rotational symmetry. This is why, above a critical temperature called the Curie temperature, thanks to thermal agitation, all the spin dipoles are randomly oriented and hence the net magnetization averages out to zero. However, below the Curie temperature, all dipoles spontaneously align in a specific direction, giving non-zero net magnetization. The Hamiltonian is still rotationally invariant, and yet magnetic dipoles select a specific direction and align. It turns out that to realize such spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics, we need to add a spin-0 field and its accompanying dynamics. How exactly the machinery of the Higgs mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking end up endowing fundamental particles with mass cannot be elaborated here. It is said that the proof of the pudding is in eating. We hope to get this far and discuss these issues. Dark Clouds: We started with bright blue skies and end with dark clouds. I wish I could end this preface on a positive

title: SOFT CONDENSED MATTER PHYSICS
scope: • Develop familiarity with the basics of soft condensed matter. • To develop an understanding about the forces and order of thermal fluctuations in soft matter. • Why some part of matter is classified as soft matter?
description: Soft matter or soft condensed matter is a subfield of condensed matter comprising a variety of physical systems that are deformed or structurally altered by thermal or mechanical stress of the magnitude of thermal fluctuations. They include liquids, colloids, polymers, foams, gels, granular materials, liquid crystals, and biomolecules. These materials share an essential characteristic feature in that predominant physical behaviors occur at an energy scale comparable with room temperature thermal energy. At these temperatures, quantum aspects are less significant. In this course, our aim would be to understand the structure, properties, and dynamics of the soft matter. What is the order of forces and times scales that affect the overall behaviour of this class of matter?

title: Group Theory and Applications
scope: • Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational concepts of group theory. • Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible components and interpret their physical significance. • Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. • Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. • Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie groups and Lie algebras.
description: This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as ‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.

title: Physics of Semiconductor Devices
scope: The objective of the course is to develop an understanding of the basic phenomenon of the semiconductor devices. The main content of the course is having theoretical description of these devices which is an essential requirement in order to understand the operational details of any device.
description: This course will discuss the physics behind the semiconductors and the devices. The structure of any solid material plays an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum theory of solids. In the later part of the course the discussion will be focused on the voltage current behavior of the devices. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed.

title: Classical and Quantum Waves
scope: ● Understand oscillatory motion: Analyze simple harmonic motion, superposition of oscillations, and the effects of damping and external driving forces, including resonance and quality factor ● Master the physics of coupled systems and waves: Explain how coupled oscillators lead to normal modes, and how taking the continuum limit gives rise to wave phenomena, including the wave equation, traveling waves, and energy transport ● Analyze wave behavior and propagation: Distinguish between group and phase velocity, and describe how waves interact with boundaries and each other through reflection, refraction, and interference ● Grasp the foundations of quantum mechanics: Explain wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and apply the Schrödinger equation to determine wavefunctions and energy quantization in simple systems ● Apply quantum tunneling to real-world technology: Calculate transmission coefficients for barrier tunneling and connect this phenomenon to practical applications such as scanning tunneling microscopy
description: This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling.

description.supporting_text: This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling.

title.supporting_text: Course Title: Classical and Quantum Waves

title: Introduction to Classical and Quantum Waves
scope: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines.
description: Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves, introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications; Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers.

title: Fundamentals of Supply Chain – Concepts
scope: The fundamentals of supply chain – concepts course is aimed at providing a solid grounding and understanding of what constitutes a supply chain, setting the stage for more advanced topics. The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insights into the various key components and concepts of the supply chain. This course will assist in understanding Supply Chain Management (SCM) not as a technology but rather a business strategy tool for the companies trying to create competitive advantage in the market. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: • Attain familiarity with the fundamental concepts of the SCM and its use in organizations. • Understand the key components of the Supply Chain and the interrelationships. • Importance of supply chain in today’s business environment and the impact of Globalization. • Supply Chain emerging trends

title: Advanced Operations Management
scope: This course details the various aspects and emerging concepts of operations management as they relate to the manufacturing/production function, maintenance, quality, and service operations. It provides a detailed view of each of the above functions, including their strategic importance, operational aspects, and roles in the supply chain. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: • This course will give students an overview of the various components of manufacturing and maintenance management as practised on the shop floor. The various kinds of manufacturing operations, the types of jobs performed, and the maintenance activities undertaken to ensure operational readiness and integration with other functions of the industry will be discussed. This will help one understand how the shop-floor execution and upkeep of resources (machines/equipment) are critical to the functioning of a coherent supply chain. • This will help the students to understand the importance of quality management. Explain the various quality management tools and techniques used in an organisation to ensure that quality products and services are produced. • This course will provide an overview of the service operations management. Customer service design, service operations and execution, and monitoring service delivery performance will be discussed.
description: Types of Manufacturing, Manufacturing, maintenance, quality and service operations management concepts. Manufacturing Management measures, Factory/plant performance, Operations Improvement framework. Maintenance management, optimising maintenance costs; Improving asset lifecycle; Preventive maintenance; Total productive maintenance (TPM); Quality management - practices and processes; Total quality management (TQM); Service Operations Management definition; Customer loyalty and satisfaction.

title: Logistics and Procurement
scope: This course will give students a broad overview of the fundamental theories regarding various logistics functions and their overall management. With this course, students will be able to approach logistics management with a holistic view and understand, analyse, and coordinate various functions within a coherent supply chain framework. • This will help students understand the various components of procurement – sourcing, contracting, supplier management, qualification management, purchasing of direct and indirect materials, spend analysis, and its integration with other management systems/applications. • This will help explore the importance of inventory management, the key components involved, and the best practices that businesses can implement to improve their inventory management processes.
description: Supply chain network design; Supply chain Relationships; Freight modes; Logistics planning; Shipment execution; Transportation sourcing and procurement; Freight Billing and Payments; Omni-Channel Distribution; Global Trade Management (GTM); Warehousing; RFID in supply chain; Warehouse Picking; Yard Management; Strategic Sourcing; Agreements, Supplier Management; Supplier Risk Management, Spend Analysis and Optimization; AI and use cases in procurement; Inventory management-Concepts and classifications; Types of Inventory Transactions; Managing Uncertainty; cost management; inventory control techniques; Product genealogy traceability and recall management; Replenishment; Material movements across facilities; CPFR concept; Project Based Supply Chain; Digital Technologies in SCM; Integration with other SCM systems.

scope.supporting_text: This course will give students a broad overview of the fundamental theories regarding various logistics functions and their overall management. With this course, students will be able to approach logistics management with a holistic view and understand, analyse, and coordinate various functions within a coherent supply chain framework. • This will help students understand the various components of procurement – sourcing, contracting, supplier management, qualification management, purchasing of direct and indirect materials, spend analysis, and its integration with other management systems/applications. • This will help explore the importance of inventory management, the key components involved, and the best practices that businesses can implement to improve their inventory management processes.

title: Management Accounting
scope: This course focuses on how cost accounting helps managers make better decisions, as cost accountants are increasingly becoming integral members of their company’s decision-making teams. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: i. This course will equip students with the knowledge and analytical skills required to apply management accounting tools and techniques for planning, decision making, cost control, and performance evaluation in organizations.
description: Success in any organization—from the smallest corner store to the largest multinational corporation—requires the use of cost accounting concepts and practices. Cost accounting provides key data to managers for planning and controlling, as well as costing products, services, even customers. Cost accounting is one of very important managerial tool for business strategy and implementation.

title: Fundamentals of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology
scope: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.
description: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.

scope.supporting_text: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.

description.supporting_text: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
